outcomes: Peel Watershed dispute settled in the Supreme Court in favor of the First Nations' appeal; a US-Canada pact imposes a 7-year moratorium on subsistence salmon harvest on the Yukon River (contested by Alaska Natives and Yukon First Nations); the 2021 Iqaluit response airlifted 750,000 L of water and used military water purification; an open-access Arctic WEF Nexus Portal was released as the practical output.
findings: In the 2024 Global WEF Nexus Index seven Arctic nations ranked among the top 12 and Iceland, Norway, Canada and the USA held the top four places, but regional scores expose large internal gaps: Labrador's water access score is 25.77 against a water availability score of 80.71, and Nunavut scores 12.76 on energy and 34.21 on food against Canada's national 77.9 (energy) and 69.9 (food) (Part 1, p. 9; Part 1, p. 15; Part 1, p. 15). || Alaska's WEF index is 62.73, about 16 points below the US score (the Summary gives 15.35); the deficit sits in food (sub-index 43.55 against 79.28 for the US; food availability 51.98 points below the US) while water and energy are only 3.87 and 6.48 points below (Part 2, p. 27; Part 2 summary, p. 35). || Using the index version applied in Part 3 (Ingram et al. 2021), northern Canada's energy pillar is 51.88 (90th globally) against Canada's 84.81 (3rd) and its food pillar is 48.22 (113th) against 73.22 (13th); energy imports are 82.5% of energy use and 85 diesel-reliant off-grid communities hold 69,477 people (43% of the study-area population) (Part 3, p. 39; Part 3, p. 39; Part 3, p. 41). || Remote residents pay far more for basic services: a healthy food basket cost $496 per week in Old Crow, Yukon against $206 in Whitehorse (currency printed only as $), with northern transport adding more than 20% and electricity rates about 84% higher (Part 3, p. 42); Alaska households without piped water use about 5.7 L per person per day against 20 L (WHO standard) and 302-379 L (US household average) (Part 2, p. 29). || The data audit found data for only about 49% of WEF-SDG indicators in northern Canada (SDG 7 67%, SDG 6 56%, SDG 2 30%) and only 61% of the data were less than 5 years old; Canada's food-insecurity indicator excludes on-reserve and other Indigenous settlements, which hold about 50% of northern residents (Part 4, p. 46; Part 4, p. 47).

outcomes: None measured. The paper reports local efforts (switching to Columbia River water; processors giving wastewater to farmers) that coincide with the modeled optimum.
findings: A linear, time-variant input-output model of 21 food-energy-water subsectors (4 water, 7 energy, 10 food) for Umatilla and Morrow counties, Oregon, gives energy intensities of 0.7 MJ/m3 (0.19 kWh/m3) for groundwater, 0.3 MJ/m3 (0.08 kWh/m3) for surface water, 2.4 MJ/m3 (0.67 kWh/m3) for wastewater and 0.1 MJ/m3 for recycled water (Table 1, p. 8). || Variation in allocation coefficients (which source supplies which user) and variation in technology coefficients produce significantly different output distributions for all nine water and electricity subsectors tested (two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic 0.028-0.431, p = 0.000; 100,000 Monte Carlo iterations), so better technology cannot fully offset allocation variability, which is largest for gas and coal because they balance the grid (Table 2, p. 10; p. 8). || Sensitivity analysis (one coefficient varied by 10% at a time) shows agriculture, especially alfalfa, corn and spring grains, is most sensitive for water and energy, and water subsectors are most sensitive for electricity (abstract; sect. 3.3, p. 10). || Multi-objective linear programming (cost and global warming potential) favors more Columbia River surface water instead of groundwater, hydroelectricity for lowest cost and wind for lowest warming potential, which matches local stakeholder moves to avoid groundwater depletion and food processors giving wastewater to farmers at no cost (sect. 3.4, p. 11). || Governance barriers appear in the results: Oregon rules do not distinguish wastewater by source and bar direct irrigation reuse unless treated, and electricity price drives crop choice (expensive power pushes farmers to low-profit wheat and barley; cheap power supports potatoes and onions) (p. 14; p. 14).

outcomes: Statutes and programs are listed as adopted but their effectiveness is not evaluated; the chapter calls for more evidence on how instruments work and combine.
findings: A survey of nexus policy instruments finds a polycentric but fragmented landscape: few instruments genuinely integrate water, energy and food, most link two sectors, and innovation is more visible at the subnational level than nationally or internationally, with US states and agencies prominent (p. 79; p. 80). || Ten US states (Texas, Arizona, California, Nevada, Colorado, Connecticut, Washington, South Dakota, Wisconsin, West Virginia) were adopting statutes to integrate water and energy; Arizona (Statute 45-156, 1999) requires a legislative act to approve water appropriation for electricity generation and Nevada (Statute 533.372) requires state-engineer approval of water used for exported power (p. 81; p. 81; p. 81). || California links water, energy and climate through the AB 32 Scoping Plan (2006), the Integrated Regional Water Management Planning Act (amended 2008) and the Water Conservation Act of 2009 (SB X7-7), which requires a 20% cut in per-capita urban water use by 2020 and makes suppliers that fail to meet agricultural water-management requirements ineligible for state grants and loans (p. 80; p. 80; p. 80). || Quasi-public utilities act as nexus innovators: Sonoma County Water Agency's 'carbon-free water' policy and the San Antonio Water System's mix of conservation, reduced distribution energy, wastewater recycling and biogas from sewage; the Chesapeake Bay Program (1983) is a federal-state partnership spanning water quality, fisheries, renewable energy and land conservation (p. 80; p. 80).

outcomes: No policy outcomes; the work fed the open-access Arctic WEF Nexus Portal (University of Saskatchewan CHASR) that lets users calculate scores for 29 regions.
findings: Alaska's WEF index is 62.73 against 78.08 for the US (gap 15.35 points; the abstract rounds to about 16): water is 3.85-3.87 points lower, energy 6.47-6.48 points lower and food 35.73 points lower (sub-index 43.55 against 79.28), so the deficit is concentrated in food (abstract, p. 3; sect. 5, p. 26; sect. 6, p. 33). || Sub-regional scores show strong internal variation: Interior has the lowest WEF score (55.30) and food availability (15.96), Far North the lowest energy access (50.01) and food access (35.13), and Southeast the highest WEF score (65.00) and energy availability (85.19) (Table 5.1, p. 26). || Water and energy insecurity are mainly access problems (water access 87.66 against 99.37 for the US, while water availability is 4.01 points above the US) and food insecurity is an availability problem (food availability 51.98 points below the US) (sect. 6, p. 33; sect. 5, p. 27). || Structural drivers are infrastructure, supply chains and fiscal choices: only 58% of Alaska communities have piped water and wastewater, households without piped water use about 5.7 L per person per day, Alaska imports 95% of its food at about US$2 billion a year, and limited in-state refining leaves rural communities dependent on imported fuel although Alaska is a major energy producer (sect. 5.1.1, p. 29; sect. 5.1.1, p. 29; sect. 5, p. 27; sect. 5, p. 27).

outcomes: Perception-based ex post results: ferry cutbacks affected 94% of Cordova participants; satisfaction with existing renewable projects ranged 42-68% and no one linked them to food-energy-water security; no formal policy evaluation.
findings: Structured interviews with 114 households (Cordova 50, Kongiganak 51, Igiugig 13) show high overall food-energy-water security (79% of responses agree with security statements; availability 82%, quality 72%, access 67%, preference 66%) but food is the weakest sector, with security lowest in Cordova (63%, after the state ferry stopped) and Kongiganak (64%) (sect. 3.1, p. 5; sect. 3.3, p. 5; sect. 3.3, p. 5; sect. 3.3, p. 6). || Store-bought and harvested food differ sharply: 24% of participants report insecurity for contemporary (purchased) food against 5% for subsistence food (Kruskal-Wallis chi-square = 236, p < 0.001), and counting both sources the authors estimate 15% food insecurity against the USDA's 10% for Alaska households in 2017-2019 (abstract, p. 1; sect. 3.3, p. 7; sect. 4, p. 9). || Most drivers of insecurity are external to the communities: costs (47% of coded responses), transportation (15%), weather and seasonality (9%), fuel costs (8%) and income (8%); 94% of Cordova participants were affected by ferry cutbacks (68% named food security or finances) and 17% and 12% of participants could not afford gasoline or home heating (sect. 3.5, p. 8; sect. 3.5, p. 8; sect. 3.3, p. 7). || Satisfaction with local renewable energy ranged from 42% to 68% (unreliability, uncertain economic benefit, wanting other or more renewables), no respondent linked their renewable program to food-energy-water security, and the state's Power Cost Equalization subsidy can work against renewables if local savings are offset by reduced subsidies (abstract, p. 1; sect. 3.4, p. 7; sect. 4, p. 9). || The three communities differ markedly: Kongiganak (95% Indigenous Yup'ik) has 97% of households without complete plumbing, 61% on SNAP and median household income of US$50,313, against 0% without plumbing and US$94,625 in Cordova; wild-food harvest is 246 kg per capita in Igiugig and 53 kg in Cordova (Table 1, p. 4).

outcomes: The index is cited in UN inter-agency policy briefs; no North American policy outcome is reported.
findings: Across 163 countries the WEF Nexus Index correlates with the Human Development Index at r = 0.81 (roughly 65% of variance), more strongly than with the Corruption Perception Index (0.73), the Human Rights Index (0.48) or the Gini coefficient (-0.33); the correlation with the planetary-pressures-adjusted HDI is 0.80 in the abstract and 0.64 in the text (abstract, p. 1; p. 6; p. 7). || Large North American countries have high national scores but wide internal ranges: HDI runs from 0.945 in Ontario to 0.834 in Nunavut within Canada (national HDI 0.939) and from above 0.960 in Massachusetts to 0.860-0.870 in Mississippi within the USA, so the authors advise supplementing national scores with subnational assessments such as those for Alaska and northern Canada (p. 10; p. 10; p. 4). || The index prioritizes domestic self-sufficiency over trade-based security and truncates net energy imports at zero so that energy exporters are not rewarded for surplus; the authors recommend that national planning commissions rather than sector ministries lead nexus work, citing the SADC regional framework as a model (p. 4; p. 2).

outcomes: Qatar (non-NA): results shared with stakeholders shifted the national narrative on self-sufficiency and the food security program became an interministerial committee. No Texas outcomes are reported.
findings: The chapter offers a 7-question guideline for nexus modeling (critical question, stakeholders, scale, system of systems, what to assess, data, communication of results) and illustrates it with the WEF Nexus Tool 2.0, which accounts for water, energy, land, carbon, financial requirements and imports under user-defined scenarios (p. 58; p. 59). || Texas expects a 40% gap in water availability by 2060 (TWDB 2012), planned to be covered 60% by conventional sources, 24% by conservation and 16% by non-conventional supply (reuse and desalination); regional planning involves 16 planning zones with voting stakeholder groups, and the framing identifies three hot spots: Lubbock (agriculture vs water), San Antonio (urban agriculture vs water) and South Texas (energy vs water) (sect. 6.4.3, pp. 63-64; p. 65). || In the Qatar case (not North America) a preliminary assessment showed that a 10% increase in self-sufficiency of a few local food products carried large water, energy, carbon and financial costs and risks, and sharing this with stakeholders changed the national narrative about self-sufficiency (p. 60; p. 62; p. 62).

outcomes: Zacatecas low-cost solar heater training program discontinued in 2017 after funding politicization; only male trainees started microenterprises; 700 free heaters distributed in 2019 in 34 municipalities but with city-based access that excluded rural elderly women; Arizona net-metering change in September 2018 reduced payments to new small generators.
findings: A feminist political ecology study of small-scale solar in urban and rural Arizona (22 interviews, 1 focus group) and Zacatecas, Mexico (11 key-informant interviews, 3 focus groups, 3 stakeholder meetings) finds most solar energy used by women is tied to water, for household chores or irrigation of urban and rural agriculture, and solar users were more likely to harvest water, compost and grow crops (a 'multiplier effect') (abstract, p. 1; p. 9). || Tucson households with solar pay US$0-65 per month for electricity against US$80-155 without (US$119 for one household leasing panels from the utility), but from September 2018 new small solar generators receive a 10-year fixed rate while earlier systems keep the retail rate for up to 20 years, which the authors call expropriation by a utility monopoly (p. 5; p. 4). || In Zacatecas installed solar water heater area grew from 154.27 m2 (2007) to 397.83 m2 (2017), saving about 21 L of LPG per household per month; 68.6% of households use water heaters against 45.3% nationally and 25% of homes have solar heaters (106,507 units through 2016), yet the 30 kg propane price rose from 366 pesos (2012) to 590 pesos (2018) (p. 4; p. 4; p. 7). || Program outcomes were uneven: a low-cost self-built heater program (materials 1,000 pesos, about US$62.82, versus about 5,000 pesos commercially) trained mostly women (12 of 15 in one group) but only male trainees started microenterprises and funding was politicized and discontinued in 2017; the state gave away 700 heaters to low-income residents in 34 municipalities in 2019 through city-based sign-up that excluded rural elderly women (p. 6; p. 6; p. 8; p. 5; p. 7). || Institutional context shaped benefits: Arizona's bottom-up non-profit projects were limited by federal housing rules (a resident's energy savings go to pay housing costs under a 34%-of-income cap) and utility net-metering changes, while the La Bufa wind park in Zacatecas gives local residents no energy subsidy and its leases bar other land uses in perpetuity (p. 6; p. 4).

outcomes: Reported by the editorial (secondary): bills with high WEF integration are not necessarily adopted and effective California policies are reactive; NIH-supported funded projects cut agricultural water use by 60% with improved clinical outcomes.
findings: Editorial for a 2026 Research Topic: Pao et al. analyzed 25 years of California legislative documents for the Salton Sea region and found that a high degree of WEF integration in a bill does not necessarily lead to adoption; the most effective policies are reactive, target environmental threats to food production and favor water-food synergies (p. 2; p. 2). || A pilot 'project/policy laboratory' program supported by the US National Institutes of Health (country not stated in the editorial) reported that funded projects cut agricultural water use by 60% and improved clinical health outcomes among vulnerable populations; baselines and location are not given (p. 2). || Other contributions are non-North American: weekly freshwater replenishment of 19% sustains optimal water quality in IoT-monitored aquaponics, and WEFE financing is held back by complex investment structures and long payback, with blended finance and insurance-backed risk-sharing proposed (p. 1; p. 2).

outcomes: SGMA (2014) and the expanded Irrigated Lands Regulatory Program are in force; SWEEP (2014) funded more than 800 projects saving 88,496 ML of water and 80,077 MTCO2e per year (as reported); no statewide rule governs pumping energy.
findings: Pumping groundwater uses 5.6% of California's energy; groundwater pumping takes 496-1,750 MJ per ML (0.14-0.49 kWh/m3), agricultural pumping uses about 10 TWh of electricity a year of which at least 1 TWh (10%) could be saved through better metering and distribution, and 8% of California's energy use is agricultural, 70% of it for groundwater pumping (abstract, p. 1; p. 2; p. 14; p. 14). || Drought converts surface-water shortage into pumping energy: the 2014 drought assessment reported an 8.1 million ML surface-water loss offset by 6.3 million ML of extra groundwater pumping at USD 454 million, and during the 2012-2016 megadrought groundwater's share of total water use nearly doubled from 30-40% to about 60% (p. 2; p. 14). || Water-saving irrigation raised energy use: about half of California's irrigated land moved from gravity to pressurized systems since 1972 (efficiency 67.5-70% for surface, 70-82.5% for sprinkler, 87.5-90% for drip), improving water efficiency but increasing overall energy consumption, while flood and furrow irrigation still covers about 40% of irrigated area (p. 14; p. 14; p. 2). || Governance is fragmented: SGMA (2014) targets groundwater sustainability by 2040-2042 and the Irrigated Lands Regulatory Program was expanded in 2014 for nitrates, yet there are no statewide regulations on energy for groundwater pumping, regulating surface water without groundwater shifts pressure to the unregulated source, and only one decision tool (AgMonitor) co-manages irrigation and energy (p. 5; p. 5; p. 16). || The State Water Efficiency and Enhancement Program (SWEEP, 2014) invested USD 80 million in over 800 projects saving 88,496 ML of water and 80,077 MTCO2e per year, but only 10% of funds reached socially disadvantaged growers although a third of projects were in disadvantaged communities (p. 15; p. 15).

outcomes: No policy outcomes; the open-access Arctic WEF Nexus Security portal (University of Saskatchewan) was released for tracking scores over time.
findings: Adapting the Global WEF Nexus Security Index to Alaska (19 of 21 indicators; wild-harvest substitutes for cereal yield and protein), the US scores 78.08 (5th of 181 nations) and Alaska 62.73, a gap of 15.35 points (about 16 in the abstract): food sub-index 43.55 against 79.28, water and energy only 3.87 and 6.48 points below (p. 78; p. 78; p. 85). || Regional scores vary widely (Table 3): Interior has the lowest WEF score (55.30) and food availability (15.96), Far North the lowest energy access (50.01) and food access (35.13), and Southeast the highest (65.00) with energy availability of 85.19 (Table 3, p. 83). || Water and energy insecurity in Alaska arise mainly from access (water access 87.66 against 99.37, while water availability is 4.01 points above the US) whereas food insecurity arises from availability (51.98 points below the US), reflecting dependence on southern supply chains, an export-driven economy and degraded infrastructure (p. 79; p. 86). || Structural drivers include infrastructure and fiscal choices: only 58% of Alaska communities have piped water and wastewater, households without piped water use about 5.7 L per person per day, Alaska imports 95% of its food at about US$2 billion a year, limited in-state refining leaves rural communities dependent on imported fuel, and under-investment in water has been attributed to prioritizing economic prudence over health (p. 80; p. 81; p. 79; p. 79; p. 81). || The index and an online Arctic WEF Nexus Security portal were developed with the advice of an Arctic Council expert group (SECEG) and an Indigenous Steering Committee (Arctic Athabaskan Council and Inuit Circumpolar Council) and are offered as a starting point for dialogue and for tracking interventions over time, not as a prescription (p. 71).

outcomes: Describes treaty and agreement regimes already in force (1909 Boundary Waters Treaty, 1964 Columbia River Treaty, 1985 Skagit Treaty, MOSPA 2016, Arctic Science Agreement 2018); no measured outcomes of nexus integration are reported.
findings: International law has no explicit WEF provisions: water, energy and food are governed by separate sectoral regimes, and the UN Watercourses Convention offers only a broad framework that does not address trade-offs among water uses such as energy and food (p. 13). || Principles that can carry a nexus approach include vital human needs first (UN Watercourses Convention Art. 10, p. 5), the human rights to water and food (p. 6), no harm (p. 8), the duty to cooperate in good faith (pp. 8–9) and the 1969 Vienna Convention rules of interpretation as a tool against legal fragmentation (p. 4). || Three North American treaties are read as WEF-relevant: the 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty (the International Joint Commission approves projects affecting boundary-water levels and flows and must weigh drinking water, hydroelectricity, agriculture and ecosystem health, p. 18); the 1961 Columbia River Treaty (hydropower and flood control, p. 17); and the 1984 Skagit River Treaty (protects the Skagit Valley in British Columbia while securing water and energy for Seattle via Ross Dam and for British Columbia via the Seven Mile Reservoir, p. 18). || For the Canadian Arctic the authors cite studies reporting high WEF insecurity, the highest Indigenous food-insecurity rates among industrialized nations, and higher water, energy and food insecurity than southern Canada and the national average, and they call for Arctic-specific WEF indicators (p. 14). || UNDRIP Arts. 26 and 32 and ILO Convention 169 Art. 15 are identified as the legal basis for Indigenous participation in WEF decisions affecting their lands, territories and waters (p. 14); two binding Arctic Council agreements are treated as relevant: the marine oil pollution agreement (MOSPA, signed 2013, in force 2016) and the Arctic Science Agreement (signed 2017, in force 2018) (pp. 16–17).

outcomes: 18 of 42 Salton Sea-focused documents became law (1999–2023), including Senate Bill 797 (2023, committee overseeing a lithium extraction tax); no bill with a WEF synergy has passed in more than a decade (p. 8).
findings: Of 42 Salton Sea-focused California bills and related documents (1999–2024, effectively 1999–2023), 18 (42.9%) were chaptered (became law) and 24 (57.1%) failed, 19 of them (79%) at the amendment stage; 0 to 6 documents were proposed per year (p. 6). || Water terms were 77.1% of WEF terms in chaptered documents, whereas failed documents were energy-heavy (energy 67.6%, water 28.6%, food 3.8%; chi-squared = 589.74, df = 2, p < 0.0001); over 25 years water was mentioned 909 times, energy 699 and food 135 (p. 6). || A high degree of WEF integration did not predict enactment: about one-third of documents contained terms from two or all three sectors, co-occurrence was unrelated to outcome (p = 0.185), and since 2014 all 15 bills with synergies between at least two sectors failed (pp. 7, 11). || Water-food synergies were the most common and most often enacted (most chaptered synergistic bills date from 2004 or earlier), water-energy synergies failed most (8 of the 15 recent failures paired them with resource-use themes), energy-food synergies were rare and always failed, and energy and food together without water never passed (pp. 7, 8, 11). || The authors read the record as reactive policy-making: enacted laws responded to threats to food production, and later public-health and lithium or geothermal bills followed lake desiccation after the 2003 Quantification Settlement Agreement shifted farm water to San Diego with fallowing that reduced runoff to the Sea and exposed the lakebed (abstract; p. 8).

outcomes: Qualitative only: one failed cross-sector effort (keeping a coal plant open) and one cooperative purchase (a power-plant unit bought by agricultural organizations); no quantified outcomes.
findings: A structured case study of Phoenix food-energy-water governance (social network of 93 stakeholders, 17 interviews, participant observation of 6 public meetings, January–June 2020) found four barrier categories: structural asymmetries, process asymmetries, coordination and communication challenges, and external influences such as histories of conflict (pp. 114–116). || The authors conclude that sector mismatch, the analogue of scale mismatch, is the main cause of the barriers: food, energy and water organizations differ in structure, decision processes, time frames and jurisdictions (abstract; p. 117). || Governance structures differ (agriculture largely decentralized, energy largely centralized in a few actors, water multi-level) and so does collaboration: water actors collaborate within and across sectors and can act as boundary organizations because water is the limiting resource; food actors mostly collaborate within the sector (for example, agricultural organizations jointly bought a unit of a local power plant); energy-only organizations collaborate with peers while combined water-energy organizations reach across sectors (pp. 113, 116, 117). || Power asymmetries matter: a small group of long-standing water interests is said to dominate Arizona water law, an energy stakeholder said energy interests were excluded from the Drought Contingency Plan process, and the historical water grievances of tribal communities shape meetings (pp. 115–116). || Stakeholders named seven enablers (building trust, shifting attitudes, finding common ground, transparency and communication, sharing resources, finding mutual benefit, and using times of crisis); foundational conditions such as trust and shared understanding must come before structural adaptation (pp. 116–117).

outcomes: Reports 2000–2001 responses: Colorado River Aqueduct pumps shut to free power, a reduced targeted salmon spill, irrigation allotment cuts (Turlock Irrigation District 1.2 m to 1.1 m, 48 to 42 in), and an executive order letting gas plants run longer; the predicted summer 2001 blackouts did not materialize (p. 77).
findings: Water pumping and treatment used more than 15,000 GWh a year, at least 6.5% of California electricity (California Energy Commission, 1999); the Department of Water Resources put pumping at 5% of peak load and 7% of total electricity use; the State Water Project alone averaged 5,000 GWh a year (2–3% of state electricity) and lifts water 587 m (1,926 ft) at the A.D. Edmonston plant; electricity was 20–80% of a water utility operating budget (pp. 76–78). || About 25% of California electricity came from hydropower (20–22% large, 3–4% small; about 6,900 MW plus 3,222 MW pumped storage), and one-third of the hydropower used in California came from the Pacific Northwest (p. 74). || In 2000–2001 the deregulation-era energy crisis (electricity rates up 300% over the past year, rolling blackouts in December 2000 and spring 2001) combined with dry conditions (California at 76% of average precipitation at the end of March 2001; the driest Northwest winter in 70 years) to force water-energy trade-offs: the Metropolitan Water District shut Colorado River Aqueduct pumps, freeing power for 100,000 homes and nearly 45% of aqueduct energy use, while the Bonneville Power Administration proposed paying irrigators to fallow 27,114–40,469 ha (67,000–100,000 acres) to avoid pumping from Grand Coulee (pp. 73, 74, 77, 78, 80, 81). || New thermal power plants add water demand: nearly half of 28 major proposed plants would use fresh water, five West Kern plants (more than 3,000 MW) would use about 19 × 10^6 m3 a year (16,000 acre-feet), and dry cooling uses 95% less water (p. 82). || Of California captured usable runoff (88 × 10^9 m3, 71 million acre-feet), agriculture used 43%, urban areas 11% and the environment 46%; the Metropolitan Water District charged USD 431 per acre-foot (1,233 m3) for treated water and USD 294 for treated agricultural water, against USD 652 for desalination (pp. 77, 83).

outcomes: Context only: in long droughts Georgia EPD suspended new permits and paid farmers not to irrigate (most recently 2013), and in 2001 took more than 13,355 ha (33,000 acres) out of irrigation at about 4.5 million USD (sect. 2.1). The study's own results are modeled, not observed.
findings: In a groundwater-dominated basin (21 Georgia counties, 1980–2010), allowing deficit irrigation while keeping crop diversity near observed acreage (scenario AQ2) raised mean annual revenue by 18.0% and profit by 51.5% over the baseline (AQ1) while cutting water pumped by 14.1% and pumping energy by 14.7% (96.5 vs 113.1 GWh) (Table 2, sect. 5.4; modeled). || Excluding deficit irrigation (AQ2-IR) raised pumped water by 36.1% (480 × 10^6 m3 vs 352 × 10^6 m3 in AQ1) and pumping energy by 35.7% (153.5 GWh) for similar revenue and profit to AQ2-M (427.4 vs 427.3 million USD; 269.9 vs 274.5); deficit irrigation therefore saves about 146 × 10^6 m3 (118,006 acre-feet) a year and 4.5 × 10^9 m3 (3.65 million acre-feet) over 31 years (Table 2, sect. 5.4; modeled). || Removing the crop-diversity constraint (AQ2-M) lifted revenue and profit by 42.8% and 132.8% over baseline in Table 2 (the text reports 40% and 128% after correcting, presumably for bias) but needed 31.5 × 10^6 m3 (25,507 acre-feet) more pumped water and 10.4 GWh more energy than AQ2; the 90.34 million USD (2010) profit difference is the modeled cost of keeping crop diversity (sect. 5.4). || Once the water table falls past a threshold depth, pumping cost exceeds the extra revenue from irrigation, so rainfed area rises and deficit-irrigated area falls; in the driest years more than 40% of acreage is under deficit irrigation and in the wettest years more than 90% is rainfed (sect. 5.5, Figs. 7–8; modeled). || Tripling energy prices (Grady County test) raises the rainfed share from 18% to 32% in dry years and from 18% to 23% in normal years and nearly halves fully irrigated corn acreage, while deficit irrigation stays economical because its trigger and application depth can be adjusted (sect. 5.6, Fig. 9; modeled).

outcomes: Plan adopted January 2019 by the borough Sustainability Commission (established 12 October 2017); the Alaska House created a food security subcommittee on 2 May 2018; implementation and effects on food security are not yet known (pp. 3, 6, 9, 12).
findings: Alaskans obtain as much as 98 percent of their food from out of state; food is a USD 5 billion a year business and Alaskans spend USD 1.9 billion a year importing it, while Alaskan farms produce about USD 15 million a year, wild foods are valued at USD 400–900 million a year and small farms sell about USD 2.2 million a year locally (pp. 2–3). || Twenty-one stakeholder interviews (22–29 July 2018) named barriers to local food supply in Fairbanks: end-of-the-road location, just-in-time grocery stocking, no cold storage or processing, a short growing season, high energy costs that make indoor farming hard, mostly public and hard-to-reach arable land, labor shortages and high prices (pp. 5, 7). || South Fairbanks is a USDA-declared food desert, and just over 4,000 people (about 4% of the population) received SNAP benefits at the end of 2017 (pp. 7, 12). || The seven-member borough Sustainability Commission adopted a plan in January 2019 with four food-security areas (agricultural workforce, food stocks, local production and sales, access to local fruits and vegetables) but no quantitative targets, and implementation depends on convincing the mayor and Assembly to fund priorities amid falling oil revenue and no state personal income or sales tax (pp. 9, 10, 12). || Public input looked mainly to individuals and the private sector rather than government, the widely repeated three-day food supply in Fairbanks is unverified, and the authors, who were participant-observers, describe the university as an honest broker converting stakeholder input into action items (pp. 4, 9).

outcomes: Describes California policy instruments (SBX7-7 Water Conservation Act, AB 32, 2014 Water Action Plan, groundwater sustainability planning); savings figures are estimates and no measured policy outcomes are reported.
findings: In 2001 the California water sector used 56,871 GWh of electricity, 19.2% of the state total of 296,203 GWh, emitting 17.4 of 90.45 MMTCO2e (2001 electricity with the 2013 emission factor of 0.3054 MTCO2e/MWh); urban water used 37,452 GWh (11.4 MMTCO2e) and agricultural water 10,560 GWh (3.4 MMTCO2e) (Table 14.1, p. 154). || Energy intensity is 3.37 kWh/m3 (4.16 MWh per acre-foot) for urban water and 0.26 kWh/m3 (0.32 MWh per acre-foot) for agricultural water because urban supply adds conveyance, treatment and end uses and agriculture relies more on gravity-fed surface irrigation; average annual use in 1998–2010 was 11.1 × 10^9 m3 (9 million acre-feet) urban and 40.7 × 10^9 m3 (33 million acre-feet) agricultural (p. 154). || Water-related uses take about 19% of the state's electricity and 32% of non-power natural gas; about 75% of the water sector's electricity is used by end users and about 25% in water and wastewater systems; conveyance intensity runs from 0 (gravity) to 3.70 kWh/m3 (14,000 kWh per million gallons) and moving water between basins can take an order of magnitude more energy than local supplies (Table 14.2, p. 156). || Meeting the SBX7-7 target (20% cut in urban per-capita use by 2020, about 2.2 × 10^9 m3 or 1.8 million acre-feet) would save an estimated 7,488 GWh and 2.29 MMTCO2e (estimated from the average urban intensity, pp. 152, 154). || The drought that began in 2012 led to more than 162,000 ha (400,000 acres) fallowed and about USD 1.5 billion in direct agricultural costs, mostly in the San Joaquin Valley; in 2014 farms pumped 6.2 × 10^9 m3 (5 million acre-feet) of groundwater to offset a 7.4 × 10^9 m3 (6 million acre-feet) surface-water cut, with subsidence, falling water tables and higher pumping energy and emissions (pp. 154, 158).

outcomes: Reports policy and program responses: Kansas Local Enhanced Management Areas (positive results cited), a 2024 deal paying the Imperial irrigation district almost USD 700 million for cuts, the EPA Mississippi River Restoration and Resiliency Strategy (2022); the paper presents no new outcome evaluation.
findings: A perspective paper with no new data illustrates the water-energy-food-climate nexus with three US cases (Ogallala groundwater depletion, Colorado River drought, Mississippi River flooding), proposes an integrated nexus and collaborative governance approach built on learning, trust and iteration, and draws two takeaways: manage unintended consequences and build justice into nexus governance (abstract; pp. 4–6). || Ogallala: pumping runs at about ten times the recharge rate and irrigation is about 90% of groundwater withdrawal; the paper states an average annual decline of 16.8 ft since the 1950s (as printed, implausible as an annual rate and to be checked against USGS), and Kansas Local Enhanced Management Areas are reported to cut overdraft with minimal impact on net farm profits (pp. 2–3). || Colorado River (seven US states, two Mexican states, thirty Tribal Nations): about 70% of the water goes to agriculture, hydropower serves more than 4 million people and drinking water about 40 million; Tribes hold senior rights to about 20% of annual flow yet take part largely symbolically; the Imperial irrigation district accepted cuts in 2024 for almost USD 700 million in federal funds (p. 3). || Mississippi: the basin supplies drinking water to more than 20 million people and produces 92% of US agricultural exports; the Gulf hypoxic zone averaged 11,131 km2 (4,298 square miles) over five years (NOAA 2024) with corn ethanol contributing; flooding burdens lower-income and Black-majority communities (pp. 3–5). || Energy and agriculture make up 6.7% and 5.5% of US GDP and have strong political advocates against water, so nexus governance meets entrenched sectoral power; Hawaiʻi retention ponds co-designed with floating solar panels illustrate a measure that reduces both flooding and energy burden (pp. 4–5).

outcomes: Reports institutional outcomes: dam relicensing process in 2024 with first Indigenous consultation since the 1950s, the Peel Watershed plan reversal challenged and won in court by First Nations, and a 2024 fishery closure; no WEF performance outcomes are measured.
findings: Document analysis of 53 legal, policy and organizational documents found that water is governed by the most institutions, then food, then energy; functions overlap heavily (redundancy) yet run in sectoral silos (modularity), which the authors read as high policy capacity with weak integrative arrangements (abstract; pp. 4, 9). || Only one binational body, the Yukon River Panel (six members per country, created under the 2002 Yukon River Salmon Agreement), operates in the basin, the International Joint Commission has no WEF guidance, and no binational WEF or water arrangement exists comparable to the Columbia River Basin (pp. 5, 7, 11). || Conflicts show sectoral priority: placer mining allotments continue despite Indigenous food-security and salmon concerns; in the 2024 relicensing of the Mayo A/B and Whitehorse dams Indigenous governments were consulted for the first time since the 1950s but Yukon Energy declined their salmon measures for cost and technical difficulty; the Peel Watershed plan was changed from 80% protected to 71% open, and First Nations challenged it (pp. 9–11). || Basin context: four hydro facilities supply 62.1% of Yukon electricity (150.4 MW), rural Interior Alaska communities harvest on average 133 kg of country food per person a year, and the Yukon mainstem was closed in 2024 to all commercial, sport and personal-use fisheries because of declining salmon returns; about 68% of the Alaskan part of the basin is federal land (pp. 3, 5). || The authors recommend using the Yukon River Panel, the Yukon River Inter-Tribal Watershed Council (73 First Nations and Tribes) and non-government agencies as coordinators, resourced agentic interventions, and a minimal formal integrative arrangement rather than only informal agreements, with the IJC and an International Watershed Board as candidate vehicles (pp. 1, 6, 11).

outcomes: Reports observed outcomes in the north: Inuvik's containerized growing system dis-adopted after two years; limited uptake of water treatment technologies despite CAD 3 billion; existing small solar systems at Fort Simpson and Vuntut Gwitchin.
findings: An expert-scored synergy matrix of 17 water, energy and food technologies (Total Interaction Score from -4 to +4, then analytic hierarchy process preferences under scale, capital-cost and environment criteria) found 20 of 30 water-energy pairs synergistic (5 trade-offs, 5 neutral), 4 of 30 food-water pairs synergistic (24 trade-offs, 2 neutral) and 19 of 36 food-energy pairs synergistic (8 trade-offs, 9 neutral) (pp. 9–10; Table 3, p. 25). || Highest synergy is between biodigesters and fish and plant by-product innovations (shared infrastructure and GHG reduction) and between greenhouses and all renewable energy technologies; the strongest trade-offs are hydroponics and aquaponics with reverse osmosis, electrocoagulation, oxidation and forward osmosis, which compete for water, electricity and land and release contaminated gray water (pp. 10–11). || Preferred water-energy-food triplets are smart irrigation with solar PV and greenhouse, smart irrigation with wind and greenhouse, and smart irrigation with biodigester and aquaponics (a closed loop reusing aquaponics water for irrigation), with the caveat that solar PV and greenhouses do not function in the northern winter and hydroelectricity and geothermal are scale- and place-limited (p. 14). || Context: northern Canada received an average USD 2.6 billion a year of investment in 2017–2021 (about 0.6% of Canada's public investment, judged insufficient), federal investment of CAD 3 billion in community water treatment has had limited uptake, Nunavut food insecurity is as high as 70% of households (Lysenko and Schott 2019), and Inuvik's containerized growing system bought in 2021 was dis-adopted after two years because costs, capacity and unreliable water and energy outweighed the synergies (pp. 3–4). || The Alaska Village Electric Cooperative (founded 1967, 57 Alaska Native communities; wind, smart meters, prepaid cards and a circuit-rider maintenance program) is proposed as a model for locally based entrepreneurial interventions in Canada; Fort Simpson (0.1 MW, NWT) and Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation (0.5 MW, Yukon, 2021) solar systems exist (pp. 15–16).

outcomes: Documents reported outcomes such as an interstate agreement (Brazil), water reserves (Peru), an adaptation plan (Colombia), and reduced pumping and water use (Central Asia), all outside North America (Table 5, p. 831).
findings: Systematic stock-take of 739 documents (648 research, 91 project) that cover all three sectors, filtered from 3,254 initial hits (Scopus 1,514; Web of Science 1,472; Google Scholar 12; 16 organization websites 256); 87% cover only water, energy, and food and water is named first in 64% (food 25%, energy 10%) (sect. 2.2.4, p. 822; Table 1, p. 823; sect. 3.1, p. 825). || North America is the focus of 8% of documents and the USA of 6% (China 8%); one study covered 69 US cities and the Columbia River basin is among the most-studied of 36 basins and aquifer systems (sect. 3.4-3.6, p. 827). || Practical outcomes are scarce: only 14 documents describe clear nexus outcomes among more than 700, drawn from solar pumping, a hydropower-funded payment-for-ecosystem-services fund for forests, water funds, and UNECE transboundary cases (sect. 3.9, pp. 828-829; Table 5, p. 831; Conclusions, p. 835). || Governance appears in 74% of documents and climate change in 66%, but stakeholder engagement in only 33%, capacity development in 15%, and gender in 9%; 42% acknowledge limitations, of which about 40% cite data (sect. 3.8 and 3.10-3.12, pp. 828-832). || Authors recommend focusing on outcomes, designing in capacity development and stakeholder engagement upstream, keeping models simple, working at basin, city, or household scale, and adding energy specialists, the least common background among nexus professionals (p. 836).

outcomes: Documented partnership outcomes: Aboriginal Caucus of seven Indigenous communities seated on the model forest Board; 2012 Recovery Strategy for Woodland Caribou after a three-year study; elk translocated from Alberta with Montreal Lake Cree Nation agreeing not to hunt until the population stabilized; Nipawin Biomass Ethanol Project agreement; diamond-mining firms agreed to involve Indigenous communities in environmental monitoring (pp. 9-10).
findings: A modified Inter-Institutional Gaps framework, interviews, one Board meeting (11 of 23 members), and PAMF documents (8 management plans, 23 project assessment reports, 7 newsletters, 5 annual reports) were used to analyze water-energy-food-forest governance in the Prince Albert Model Forest (about 360,000 ha, about 50,000 residents of whom about 20,000 are First Nations or Métis) (pp. 2, 5-6). || Six types of institutional gaps between state and non-state institutions were found (legal pluralism, cultural mismatch, institutional void, structural hole, and two intra-institutional gaps), for example no policy direction for Indigenous engagement, no long-term tenure security for non-timber forest product collection, and sector-specific forest, energy, and agriculture policies without integrative planning (Table 2, p. 8). || Energy and forest policies conflict in practice: federal sustainable forest management rules restrict low-quality wood and forest biomass available for bioenergy, and provincial renewable-energy promotion is held back by inadequate grid connectivity and unsupportive net-metering rules, against a federal net-zero 2050 commitment and a provincial plan for 50% of energy production from renewables by 2030 (p. 7). || The model forest, as a boundary organization, keeps gaps latent through ad hoc partnerships (an Aboriginal Caucus of seven Indigenous communities on its Board; a caribou study leading to a 2012 recovery strategy; the Nipawin Biomass Ethanol Project agreement), but these gaps can resurface if it stops functioning and it has no authority to settle land disputes (pp. 4, 9-11).

outcomes: State responses described: AB 32 (2006) GHG targets, the State Water Project Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reduction Plan (2012), the California Water Action Plan (2014), and the Delta Smelt Resiliency Strategy (2016); no measured outcomes are reported.
findings: California is projected to warm 4 to 9 °F (about 2.2 to 5 °C) by 2100 with 48-65% loss of snow water content by end of century; mean temperature already rose 1.1 to 2 °F (about 0.6 to 1.1 °C) over the past century, and the shift from snow to rain could affect one third of the state water supply, undermining infrastructure built on historical hydrology (pp. 1-2, 6-7). || The system manages over 40,000,000 acre-feet per year (about 49 km3), serves over 30 million people and irrigates nearly 6 million acres (about 24,300 km2); agriculture uses about 40% of available water, urban uses 10%, and the environment 50% (pp. 6, 8). || The State Water Project greenhouse gas plan adopted in 2012 aims to cut annual emissions by more than 1 million metric tons by 2020 and more than 2 million by 2050 by ending a coal-fired power contract, adding renewables, and improving efficiency; AB 32 (2006) sets statewide GHG targets (p. 8). || The multi-year drought since 2012 led to more than 400,000 acres (about 1,620 km2) of fallowed farmland, mostly with revenue losses in the San Joaquin Valley, and 95% egg-to-fry mortality of winter-run salmon in 2014 because of warm incubation water (p. 9). || Trade-offs are named across the chain: drip irrigation may use more energy to save water, biofuels carry larger water footprints and compete with food crops for land and water, and in the Delta (over 700 fish and wildlife species) restoration actions cover more than 1,100 acres (about 4.5 km2) of managed wetlands while over 700,000 acres (about 2,830 km2) of diked wetlands are private farmland, a restoration-versus-farming trade-off (pp. 9-12).

outcomes: Reported program results: Nutrition North Canada has subsidized northern retailers since 2011, including 21 million dollars (32% of budget) to ship 7.4 million kg of fruit and vegetables, but a government review found volumes and delivery times remained highly variable (p. 4).
findings: Scoring 21 SDG targets (SDG 2: 8; SDG 6: 8; SDG 7: 5) gives 210 pairwise interactions for northern Canada: 12 were negative, 15 neutral, 3 scored below -1, and 132 above +1, so about 87% were synergistic of some magnitude, compared with 166 synergies and 26 trade-offs in the global assessment by Fader et al. (2018) (p. 6). || All negative interactions involve at least one food (SDG 2) target because ending hunger, ending malnutrition, and raising agricultural productivity all require scarce land, water, electricity, and fuel (p. 6). || About 74% of communities in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut rely on trucked water and waste services (16% piped systems, 10% buckets, privies, or a mix); in Nunavut 13% of residents say water is generally unsafe and 21% unsafe at least some of the time, and seven NWT communities had boil-water advisories in 2018 (p. 2). || The three territories produce less than 1% of Canadian electricity; Yukon gets 95% from hydro with five diesel-only communities, the NWT about 75% from hydro (26 of 33 communities connected) but only 39% hydro and 57% diesel in low-precipitation 2017, Nunavut burns about 55 million liters of diesel a year, and NWT rates reach about 30 cents per kWh (pp. 3-4). || Food in Nunavut costs about 140% more than in southern Canada, a healthy food basket costs 496 dollars per week in Old Crow, Yukon versus 206 in Whitehorse, and 70% of Inuit preschoolers in Nunavut live in food-insecure households; transport (over 20%) and electricity rates (about 84% higher) drive costs (p. 4).

outcomes: Institutional outcomes reported: WEF nexus adopted at the 2011 World Economic Forum in Davos, DOE 2017 Report to Congress recognizing energy-water risk, and NSF INFEWS launched; project-level results are described qualitatively.
findings: Work in Texas Region L addresses a projected 40% water gap for Texas through three hotspots: Lubbock (falling water table from farm over-pumping; dryland farming encouraged), San Antonio (municipal growth; low-impact development with recharge and urban agriculture), and the Eagle Ford Shale (shale development raises groundwater use, concentrated in space and time) (p. 4). || During the peak of hydraulic fracturing in Texas, water for fracturing was taken from domestic and agricultural uses, and the roads used to haul fracturing water are also the community lifeline, affecting traffic and transport safety (p. 3). || The Matagorda County tool shows annual income could rise by as much as 32 million dollars above business as usual, mainly in water-short agriculture, while a nuclear plant cooling demand competes with other sectors (Kulat et al. 2019, as reported) (pp. 3, 5). || The Energy Portfolio Assessment Tool shows some energy policies cut emissions even after a capacity increase while cutting water withdrawal volume by almost 10%, whereas one technology policy (labeled CPP, not defined in the paper) raises water consumption by 5%, land use by 143%, and cost by 18% (Mroue et al. 2019, as reported) (p. 5). || Policy makers and industry leaders endorsed the nexus readily but asked for implementation guidance, demonstration, and success stories; milestones include the World Economic Forum Water Security Council (2009), adoption at Davos (January 2011), the US DOE 2017 Report to Congress on energy's dependence on water, and the NSF INFEWS program (pp. 1-2).

outcomes: Observed 1985-2009 changes reported from state water-delivery data: groundwater share of supply fell from 47% to 27%, reclaimed water rose from 2% to 9%, and per-capita municipal use fell from 1.2 to 0.9 m3 per day, which the paper links to water conservation policies; the Phoenix AMA was created under the 1980 Groundwater Management Code to control groundwater overdraft (pp. 3, 5).
findings: From 1985 to 2009 total supply stayed near 2,800 hm3 per year while groundwater fell from 47% to 27% of supply, Salt River Project water from 51% to 39%, CAP rose to nearly 20%, and reclaimed water from 2% to 9%; irrigation demand fell from 1,561 hm3 (57%) to 908 hm3 (33%) as cropland halved (about 1,400 to 700 km2), while municipal demand rose from 782 to 1,318 hm3 and water for electricity from 19 to 104 hm3 (pp. 4-5). || In the business-as-usual scenario to 2069 (population near 10 million; per-capita use 0.9 to 0.4 m3 per day) municipal demand peaks at 1,625 hm3 in 2036 (+23%) then falls to 1,224 hm3, agricultural demand falls 62% to 350 hm3 by 2028, median groundwater use falls 23% to about 593 hm3, and cumulative net recharge peaks near 2,792 hm3 around 2035 (pp. 7, 9, 11). || Keeping cropland (CropSlow, CropConst) triples food (wheat) production but raises peak groundwater use by 30% and 83% over business as usual and energy for water by up to 15%, leaving cumulative net recharge of -3,103 and -16,611 hm3 by 2069; a megadrought (Salt River Project inflows -19%, Colorado River -12%) raises groundwater use by up to 30%, energy for water by 5%, and drives net recharge to -8,037 hm3 (pp. 12-13). || A 50% renewable standard by 2030 with solar photovoltaics (Renewable scenario) cuts power-plant water demand to 74 hm3, cuts groundwater use by nearly 40%, keeps safe-yield, allows a ten-fold increase in recharge, and trims energy for water by 2%; Sustainability Index values are +2.5 (Renewable), -1.8 (CropSlow), -4.4 (Shortage), and -8.5 (CropConst) (pp. 8, 12-13). || Keeping all cropland (CropConst) gives a lower Sustainability Index (-8.5) and larger cumulative net recharge deficit (-16,611 hm3) than the megadrought scenario (-4.4; -8,037 hm3), and across scenarios 7% to 33% more water from energy-intensive sources is needed (abstract, p. 1; pp. 12-13).

outcomes: Reported program outcomes: seed funding from the university nexus initiative led to competitive NSF INFEWS awards, and a nine-paper special issue and a set of twelve recommendations were produced (pp. 106-107, 110).
findings: A reflection on a three-year, university-wide program with six sub-groups (data and modeling, energy for water, governance and financing, trade-off analysis, water for food, water for energy) that introduces a nine-paper special issue; defining the study boundary (Region L, hydrologic, aquifer, or governance boundaries) was itself a governance question (pp. 105-107). || Special-issue results summarized: low impact development for agriculture in San Antonio could add 47 billion gallons (about 178 million m3) of supply at potentially high cost, and a questionnaire to 289 public water officials (101 responses) found modest communication among water institutions and very low communication between water and food or energy institutions, with nearly 70% of agencies working to raise water reuse by up to 10% (pp. 109-110). || Treated wastewater is a suitable irrigation alternative to groundwater in West Texas (it degraded soil no more than groundwater and gave higher yields, though both lowered water-holding capacity in lower soil horizons), and the social costs of shale development (water use, emissions, transport) are hard to quantify compared with its economic benefits (p. 109). || Twelve recommendations include a coordinated stakeholder engagement plan, industry partnerships and data sharing, a national WEF community of science, a data web portal, and a town hall each semester; seed funding led to competitive NSF INFEWS awards (pp. 106-107).

outcomes: A federal appeals court vacated the US EPA stipulation on cellulosic biofuel volumes in January 2013 (note a, p. 63); otherwise the paper documents the ACF conflict context rather than evaluated outcomes.
findings: Globally about 70% of freshwater withdrawals go to agriculture and almost 10% to energy, and irrigation consumption equals one third of all blue water withdrawn; median blue-water use is 2,900 km3/yr withdrawn and 1,200 km3/yr consumed for food crops versus 568 and 25 km3/yr for thermoelectric power (p. 50; Table 1, p. 51). || In the ACF Basin (US Southeast), public supply rose from under 10% of withdrawals in 1970 to over 30% in 2005, and total withdrawals grew about 35% over 1970-2005 against about 10% nationally; wastewater discharge rose by more than 80% over 1990-2005 (p. 53-54). || In ACF drought years, two-way links become three-way competition because irrigation peaks in summer, when Apalachicola Bay oysters need fresh water and thermoelectric and hydroelectric plants run at full output to meet cooling demand (p. 54). || Conventional supply-side management in the ACF lacks broad acceptance, environmental stakeholders are often excluded, and few interstate water agreements include clauses for temporal changes in flow; the authors recommend reversible, experimental actions and integrated water-energy management with a range of stakeholders (p. 54). || The authors argue that water is the proximate driver of water-food-energy interactions, and that stressors (population, economic growth, weather and climate) and limiters (politics, norms, spatial and temporal distribution) turn pairwise links into three-way interactions (abstract, p. 49).

outcomes: Allocation policies and local management areas have not stopped depletion; many areas 'manage for depletion'. After Kansas sued Nebraska and Colorado in 1999 under the 1942 Republican River Compact, the US Supreme Court held that groundwater use depleting interstate streamflow can be restricted, and Nebraska imposed a well moratorium, mandatory metering, certified acreage and pumping limits. A Twin Platte Natural Resources District groundwater permit trading market began in 2014 (too recent to evaluate).
findings: Irrigated acreage kept expanding after Kansas farmers adopted low-pressure LEPA-type center pivots (under 5% of systems before 1990, almost 65% by 2010): total irrigated acreage in 1997-2003 exceeded 1990-1996 by 11% (Northern High Plains), 19% (Central) and 14% (Southern), so efficiency gains did not reduce withdrawals (sect. 4.6, Table 1, p. 994-995). || Depletion is concentrated in the Central and Southern High Plains: about 410 km3 has been removed since predevelopment, saturated volume has fallen about 30% (Central) and 50% (Southern) since the late 1930s, and irrigable area (more than 10 m saturated thickness) is projected to drop below half the Southern and Central areas by 2025 and 2065 (sect. 3.2, 4.4, p. 990, 993). || Irrigation raises yields two to four times over dryland (irrigated corn about 5,000 kg/ha more), and irrigation water-use efficiency nearly tripled for corn over 45 years, which raises rather than lowers the incentive to irrigate (sect. 4.2, 4.8, p. 992, 995). || Indirect policy can raise water demand: the 2005 Renewable Fuel Standard (28 billion L, or 7.5 billion US gallons, of renewable fuel by 2012) raised corn profitability, and irrigated corn now accounts for over 50% of all High Plains irrigation, while Farm Bill supports and crop insurance shift crop choice toward water-intensive crops (sect. 4.3, 5.3, p. 992, 997). || Groundwater governance is fragmented across four legal doctrines and local management areas, many of which 'manage for depletion'; the Republican River Compact case led Nebraska to impose a well moratorium, metering, certified acreage and pumping limits assessed on five-year running averages (sect. 5.1-5.2, p. 996).

outcomes: Water services resumed only after the advisory was lifted on 10 December 2021, more than two months after the first reports; Nunavut spent $9 million in emergency funds. Further advisories followed (February 2023 sewer backflow in Iqaluit; power-linked emergencies in Kinngait and Arviat in 2023), and the territorial water subsidy was reinstated in March 2024 (p. 365-368).
findings: Fuel contamination of Iqaluit piped water (odor reported 2 October 2021, contamination confirmed 12 October, advisory lifted 10 December) cascaded into emergency water supply, displaced food freight and strained health care; the authors attribute the fuel-tank damage to permafrost instability, while the city account cites failure of a structural void after about 60 years (abstract, p. 360; p. 365). || The emergency response was energy-intensive: more than 1.5 million L of bottled water arrived on 39 chartered flights (over 900,000 L by Canadian North alone) at 5.2-10.2 MJ per liter, about 2,000 times the energy of tap water, and air cargo was prioritized for water over food (p. 365-366). || Nunavut spent $9 million in emergency funds in October-December 2021, $6.9 million on bottled water; the community food center served 450-500 residents against 245 normally, and southern medevacs cost about $40,000 per patient (p. 366, 368). || Baseline fragility amplified the shock: Iqaluit imports over 60 million L of diesel a year in a July-November shipping window, food costs two to three times the national average, and about 50% of Nunavut households are food insecure (26% moderately, 24% severely); similar failures occurred in Kinngait and Arviat in 2023 (p. 364, 367). || Separate institutions and a reactionary response were the governance problem: a territorial transfer of about $2 million a year for water-infrastructure maintenance was used as a consumer subsidy (revoked 2017, reinstated March 2024, cutting trucked-water bills from $146 to $51 a month), and the authors call for interlinked, redundant WEF infrastructure planning and systems-based decision-making (p. 368-369).

outcomes: Observed outcomes of existing policy: new well permits have been closed by CONAGUA yet pumping beyond permits persists; desalination has spread to 54 private plants; groundwater councils (Consejos de Cuenca, late 1990s) have had limited effectiveness; the 2015 labor strike raised daily minimum wages from about MX$120 to MX$150-180; a public seawater desalination plant with binational financing has been commissioned.
findings: Observed: the four San Quintín aquifers are over-allocated, with concessions of 113.0 Mm3 against recharge of 69.5 Mm3, outflows of 87.5 Mm3 and an annual change of -18.0 Mm3; agriculture is about 78% of outflows, seawater has intruded, and surveyed plants reported 17,000-28,000 mg/L total dissolved solids (sect. 3.2.1, Table 1). || Fifty-four private reverse-osmosis plants (1.358 m3/s installed, 2016) desalinate about 37.9 Mm3 a year, roughly 55% of estimated agricultural water use (68.6 Mm3), using an estimated 75,873-189,683 MWh a year at 2-5 kWh/m3 and emitting 44,158-110,396 t CO2 a year, excluding well pumping (sect. 3.2, Table 2). || Energy subsidies sustain the system: the federal Tarifa 09 irrigation rate (US$0.029/kWh, December 2016) implies a subsidy of at least 28.8% and about 40% against the intermediate tariff, so electricity costs US$2.2-5.5 million a year instead of US$3.9-9.7 million (2.7-6.9% of revenue unsubsidized); SAGARPA also subsidizes construction by up to 50% (sect. 3.3.1). || Equity cost: four export crops earned about MX$2.76 billion (US$141 million) in 2016, a virtual water transfer to the US market, while Indigenous Mixtec, Zapotec and Triqui migrant farmworkers live in colonias where 66% of homes lacked drainage and 22% piped water (2010) and households pay US$8.20-15.40 a month (2.02-4.56% of income) for about 33 L per person per day (sect. 3.1-3.3). || Governance gap: private desalination is enabled by energy subsidies, capital subsidies and weak groundwater regulation, whereas public seawater desalination (250 L/s, about US$44.9 million, with up to US$34 million of North American Development Bank support) lacks such subsidies; the authors propose a managed phase-out of private energy subsidies, metering, pumping taxes for managed aquifer recharge, and wage standards through USMCA (sect. 3.3.2, 4).

outcomes: Observed 2019-2020 changes after pandemic restrictions: national electricity consumption fell about 5.6%, the nexus security index rose in 21 states and fell in 11, the global index rose in 13 states, and the Mexican economy contracted 8.5%; the authors caution that these changes cannot be entirely attributed to COVID-19.
findings: Observed 2019 versus 2020: the WEF nexus security index improved in 21 of 32 states (65.6%; Tabasco +3.9%) and fell in 11 (34.4%; Chihuahua -2.9%), while the global WEF index (adding GDP per capita and population) improved in only 13 states (40.6%) and 96.8% of states scored below 0.5; the authors state that the differences cannot be entirely attributed to COVID-19 (abstract; sect. 6). || Resource-rich states can be service-poor: Chiapas, Oaxaca, Nayarit and Michoacán have the highest nexus security because renewable generation exceeds consumption, yet Chiapas and Oaxaca have low household access to water, electricity and nutritious food, while Mexico City has the lowest scores (0.466 in 2019, 0.464 in 2020) with four of nine indicators at zero, generating 512.8 hm3 of water against 603.8 hm3 concessioned and 985 GWh of electricity (about 8% of its consumption) (sect. 6). || Water-for-energy and agricultural deficits drive state results: Guerrero had 3,655.12 hm3 (2019) and 3,199.64 hm3 (2020) of water against 4,505.98 hm3 concessioned, 69.3% of it for the Plutarco Elías Calles thermoelectric plant (18,081 GWh), and Veracruz had 4,407.15 and 4,304.5 hm3 against 6,029.27 hm3 concessioned, 64.2% agricultural (sect. 6). || The pandemic shifted resource use: national electricity consumption fell from 218,929.62 GWh (2019) to 206,564.08 GWh (2020) (commercial -10.8%, medium companies -8.1%, large industry -5.6%, residential +6.4%, agricultural +10.8%), 46.8% of states lost water availability and 56.2% lost food availability, 2019-2020 brought below-average rainfall and a +1.4 degrees C anomaly (warmest since 1953), and GDP fell 8.5% (sect. 6).

outcomes: Observed in the 2015 inventory: 41.2% of wastewater was treated inside the city, Atotonilco WWTP has operated since 2017 (82% of capacity in 2021), only 11% of compost was used, and the five landfills capture and flare biogas without energy recovery.
findings: An organizational life cycle assessment (2015 reference year) shows that activities outside Mexico City account for 13-60% of its water-food-energy impacts across eight categories; assessing only direct activities would underestimate terrestrial acidification by 60%, climate change by 49% and ozone formation by 34% (abstract; p. 5, Fig. 3). || Upstream climate impacts per capita are energy 1,397 kg CO2eq (64%), food 694 (32%) and water 90 (4%), with electricity generation the largest single contributor (43%) because 80% of national electricity was fossil-based in 2015 (p. 6, Fig. 4a-b). || Direct climate impacts are 99% fuel combustion (2,266 kg CO2eq per capita), 80% of it from transport (1,845 kg CO2eq per capita); the authors warn that electrifying transport before decarbonizing the electricity mix would only shift impacts from direct to indirect (p. 7, Fig. 5; p. 12). || Mexico City uses 977.6 Mm3 of water a year, 67.5% from the overexploited Valley of Mexico aquifer and 31.8% from Lerma-Cutzamala (1,100 m lift over 126 km); of 110 m3 per capita demanded, 74 m3 comes from the aquifer, and food dominates indirect water consumption (67%, 85 m3 per capita) (p. 3, 7-8). || Only 41.2% of wastewater was treated inside the city in 2015, about 70% of untreated flow irrigated the Mezquital Valley, and the Atotonilco plant (operating since 2017) mitigates 95% (38 m3 per capita) of water-consumption impacts and 99.8% of freshwater eutrophication; compost use is only 11% of production, limiting avoided fertilizer impacts (p. 3, 9-11, Fig. 6).

outcomes: Observed adoption remains low: battery electric vehicles were 1.9% of sales in 2019 and 45,249 electric and hybrid vehicles were registered in 2022; the review reports that the 2008 Bioenergetics Act, the 2012 General Law on Climate Change and the 2015 Energy Transition Law frame policy but that fragmented, short-cycle governance limits whole-economy decarbonization (sect. 4.2, 5.2).
findings: A PRISMA systematic review of 48 Mexico-specific articles on energy, mobility and circular economy transitions finds the most frequent resource code overlaps are energy-climate (150), energy-water (149), energy-waste (91) and energy-material (80), against energy-food (73) and water-food (58); the authors treat the energy-material (waste)-climate nexus as central, and note that 51% of energy-water overlaps concern other topics such as the WEF nexus (sect. 4.3, 5.1, Table 4). || Where energy and water meet, the literature points to water demand for green hydrogen electrolysis (roadmaps do not address water stress) and to lithium mining in the Sonora region, which faces severe water shortage and where communities voice concerns; lithium demand is projected to be 42 times higher in 2040 than in 2020 (sect. 5.1.2-5.1.3). || Regime lock-in is strong: imported natural gas supplied the largest share of Mexican electricity in 2023 (57.8%), solar and wind only 13.75%, and low-cost US shale gas is described as hindering clean energy adoption, while transport takes about 40% of final energy (sect. 4.2, 4.3). || Fragmented climate policy, short governance cycles and institutional silos are named as barriers; recommendations include long-term cross-sectoral plans coordinated through the National System of Climate Change and SEMARNAT, expanded multi-stakeholder platforms, safeguards for low-income groups and Indigenous communities (Yaqui and Seri are listed as stakeholders), and balanced management of critical minerals (sect. 5.2).

outcomes: Observed drought impacts rather than policy outcomes: in Sonora, water-scarcity events have reduced sown area by more than 160,000 ha, and Hermosillo has had to transport water from other regions when its dams reached minimum levels (p. 1687-1688).
findings: Drought is the main threat: in Hermosillo a drought (medium risk, 15% probability) gives a resilience index of 0.85 and an imposed cost of US$42.0 million in 2019 rising to US$59.5 million in 2030; in Monterrey drought (56% probability of high risk) gives 0.44 and US$269.0 million rising to US$385.0 million, and low temperatures (55% probability of medium risk) give 0.45 and US$264.2 million rising to US$378.1 million, while hurricanes are minor (p. 1689-1690, Tables 8-9). || Total potential imposed costs of nexus service failure rise 41.52% in Hermosillo (US$280.1 to 396.4 million) and 43.10% in Monterrey (US$480.4 to 687.5 million) between 2019 and 2030, with water cost up 22.33% (Hermosillo) and 20.40% (Monterrey), food cost up about 15% in both and energy penalty cost down 38.28% as renewables grow (p. 1689, Tables 5-7). || Hermosillo has the greatest water-supply problem of the cities studied: dams sit at minimum levels in droughts, water is moved from other regions of high agricultural production whose irrigators demand that their rights be respected, about 70,093 km2 of Sonora (38%) is in permanent drought, and scarcity has cut sown area by more than 160,000 ha (p. 1686-1688). || The resilience index combines a three-dimensional matrix of functional services (water in m3, energy in MW, food in tons) with penalty costs and CENAPRED risk indices; risk levels are held constant through 2030, so the projected rise comes from population growth and unit costs (p. 1685, 1689).

outcomes: Observed trends in the index: water access rose from 2013 to 2015 as drinking-water distribution systems expanded, electricity access reached 0.988 in 2019 as distribution networks grew, and food access and sustainability improved in 2019 as undernourishment and food imports fell, while no actions were seen that improved availability; the authors note that no actions appeared to be implemented between 2013 and 2015 to improve the weakest indicators (p. 13742).
findings: Observed Sonora baseline: 60 aquifers of which 18 are overexploited, annual recharge of about 3,279 hm3 against extraction of 3,313.482 hm3 (deficit of 33.982 hm3), water requirements of about 7,293 hm3 a year (agriculture 6,390, domestic 771, industry 115, non-hydro electricity 16) and agricultural water-use efficiency of only 38% (p. 13739-13740). || A nine-indicator WEF Security Index (availability, access and sustainability for each sector, tied to SDGs 2, 6 and 7) for 2013, 2015, 2019 and projections to 2025 and 2030 finds that access to water, energy and food is not at risk (electricity access 0.988 in 2019) but the nexus is unsustainable because Sonora imports water, energy and food; in-state energy capacity covers only about 14% of the state's energy consumption (p. 13742-13743, Table 7). || Water transfers cause conflict: Hermosillo's local reservoirs are drained, an aqueduct brings water from the El Novillo dam on the Yaqui River, and Yaqui Valley irrigators in the Obregón area claim the dam under irrigation rights; the authors call transfers a transitional, expensive and energy-intensive solution and recommend loss reduction, tariff revision, demand management and a review of water governance (p. 13738-13739, 13744). || Sonora SDG scores show relative strength in water and sanitation (SDG 6: 94.0) but weakness in zero hunger (SDG 2: 68.3) and clean energy (SDG 7: 62.9, with renewables only 5.3% of final energy consumption), and the lowest scores on life on land and the social goals (Table 8, p. 13744-13745).

outcomes: Observed responses reported: New York created a Building Resiliency Task Force after Sandy and set an 80% emissions reduction target for 2050; Boulder pledged an 80% emissions cut by 2050 and 100% renewable electricity by 2030; Mexico City launched its 2008-2012 climate action program and a 2011 climate law; after the Boulder flood irrigation ditch companies restored diversion works before the next growing season (sect. 3.2, 4.1).
findings: Hurricane Sandy (October 2012) cascaded through New York's transport, power and food systems (53 deaths, about US$19 billion in losses, a 4 m storm surge, 2.2 million people without power): road and tunnel closures broke food supply chains that had been restructured in the 1980s toward distant sources and small retailer inventories, whereas gravity-fed water supply and watershed land protection limited water-energy risks, although drinking-water turbidity exceeded legal limits (sect. 4.1, 4.2). || Boulder's September 2013 flood (431.8 mm in five days, 85% of the 525 mm annual average) killed 10 people regionally, forced 18,000 evacuations and destroyed 688 homes; redundant water plants, staff improvisation and shutdown of about 1,900 oil and gas wells limited cascades, yet at least 83,000 L (22,000 gallons) of oil reached waterways (sect. 4.1). || Mexico City's 2009 drought (rains three months late) affected about 49% of inspected farmland, led to more than US$100 million in emergency crop insurance and forced water restrictions in 11 districts, because the city extracts 19.1-22.2 m3/s from its aquifer and depends on Cutzamala and Lerma water pumped over 1,000 m to a city more than 100 km away at 2,200 m above sea level (sect. 4.2). || Risk is inequitably distributed: 81.2% of people affected by drought in Mexico City live in Netzahualcóyotl, water trucks served richer western areas first, the Cutzamala transfer affects the agricultural livelihoods of Indigenous Mazahua communities, and climate change may cut water availability by 10-17% (sect. 2.2, 4.2). || Governance and path dependency decide whether interdependent infrastructure amplifies or dampens cascades; the authors argue that arrangements such as Mexico City's can fail even under high-probability, lower-impact extremes and that WEF security raises justice questions about who bears risk and cost (sect. 5).

outcomes: Policy outcomes reported from the sources: the Mississippi River/Gulf of Mexico Hypoxia Task Force, established in 1997 to reduce the dead zone, is not on track to meet its goals and the dead zone has grown, a result linked to reliance on voluntary conservation; Texas and New Mexico remain in dispute over cross-border water sales.
findings: An integrative review of 42 news and grey-literature articles (2012-2024) coded into four themes (Permian Basin 18 articles, water markets 12, dead zone 11, biosolids 5) yields 200 primary-impact and 102 secondary-impact links; water is central, driving 102 tensions and receiving 125 primary impacts that cascade mostly to food (82 secondary impacts) (Results, Table 2). || State governments (44 references), oil and gas (36), farmers and ranchers (31), the fertilizer industry (26) and the federal government (22) most often drive tensions, while community stakeholders (71), farmers and ranchers (41), Gulf stakeholders (30) and oil and gas (23) are most impacted; Texas drives 68 tensions and receives 79, Florida 48 and 31 (Tables 3-4). || The Gulf dead zone ranked among the three largest in the world in 2024, nutrient loads come largely from Great Plains and Midwest agriculture, and the Mississippi River/Gulf of Mexico Hypoxia Task Force (established 1997) is described as not on track, with critics citing reliance on voluntary conservation rather than enforceable nutrient limits (Discussion, Table 5). || In the Permian Basin the Ogallala Aquifer is consumed about 10 times faster than it recharges, fracking water demand and produced-water injection are rising, and landowners increasingly sell water rights to oil and gas across state lines, while New Mexico argues that Texas takes its water (Discussion, Table 5).

outcomes: Built or contracted projects are described: two 10 MW FNPA solar projects, the 1.6 billion CAD Wataynikaneyap line owned by 22 First Nations, CIRI's 17.6 MW wind farm under a 25-year PPA, and AVEC wind-diesel systems; no ex post evaluation is given.
findings: Canada has more than 280 off-grid diesel communities (about 200,000 people), 144 of them Indigenous, so Indigenous Peoples (about 5% of the population) account for about 50% of off-grid diesel communities (p. 191). || Remote electricity is very costly: in Nunavut unsubsidized rates are 56.7 cents/kWh in Iqaluit and 112.3 cents/kWh in Kugaaruk (28.4 cents/kWh subsidized for the first 700-1,000 kWh per month) versus 14.5 cents/kWh in Saskatchewan (NEB 2018; pp. 191-192). || Indigenous ownership works at scale: Saskatchewan's First Nations Power Authority (2011) secured two 10 MW solar projects, the 1.6 billion CAD Wataynikaneyap line connects 17 off-grid Northern Ontario communities and is owned by 22 First Nations (diesel savings over 1 billion CAD in 40 years), CIRI's 17.6 MW Fire Island wind farm serves about 7,000 homes, and AVEC serves 57 Alaska Native communities (pp. 193-195). || Alaska has about 90 electric utilities and no connection to the North American grid; its electricity mix is about 45% natural gas, 25% hydro and 15% oil (EIA 2018), consumers pay nearly double the US average for energy, and the authors doubt the goal of 50% renewable electricity before 2025 will be met (pp. 194-195). || A four-pattern typology (opposed utility-scale; Indigenous-owned utility-scale of about 10 MW or more; government-driven community-scale; community-driven projects under about 1 MW) places Canada in all four, Alaska in (b) and (d), and Russia and the Nordic countries mainly in (a) and (c); patterns (b) and (d) deliver the most energy justice (p. 190).

outcomes: Muskrat Falls and Site C proceeded despite opposition (Site C still faces litigation) and British Columbia adopted a carbon tax in 2008; no impact evaluation is reported.
findings: Muskrat Falls (Labrador) is promoted as a provincial decarbonization solution, but downstream Inuit, Innu and NunatuKavut communities fear methylmercury from flooded vegetation contaminating fish and game that remain central to diets where food costs and food insecurity are serious; protest included hunger strikes and arrests (p. 174). || British Columbia draws about 95% of its power from renewables (about 85% hydro; NEB 2018), yet the WAC Bennett Dam (1960s; Williston Reservoir, described as the world's seventh largest) flooded Kwadacha territory without consultation, and Site C on the Peace River is opposed by Indigenous groups, farmers and environmentalists and faces litigation from West Moberly and Prophet River First Nations (pp. 174-175). || Part of Site C's electricity is expected to serve liquefied natural gas export, so renewable expansion may support fossil-fuel growth, and sunk costs make megaprojects hard to stop once started (p. 175). || Small community-led projects (T'Sou-ke First Nation solar; Haida Gwaii diesel reduction) draw far less conflict because decisions are local and higher governments mainly supply funding (p. 176).

outcomes: Descriptive production and export statistics; the Nutrition North Canada subsidy (about 65 million CAD per year; 121 eligible communities in 2018) and land-claim rules are described as policy context without program evaluation.
