findings: Marine products made up 89% (3,470,745 t) of northern Canada's food exports since 1988, worth more than 18 billion CAD (about 600 million CAD per year) shipped to 133 destinations, and commercial fishery revenue rose from 709 million CAD (2010) to 798 million CAD (2019) (p. 251). || The Canadian Arctic fish harvest rose from 1,924.7 t/yr (1950) to 3,286.9 t/yr (1960), fell to about 850 t/yr by the early 1990s and was 993.6 t in 2018 (pp. 251-252). || Nutrition North Canada averages a 65 million CAD annual subsidy (121 eligible communities in 2018); subsidized imports are often cheaper than northern-produced food, and most comprehensive land claims prohibit commercial sale of traditional foods (the Nunavut Agreement of 1993 is the exception), which constrains local food enterprise (pp. 256-257). || Yukon had 142 farms on 10,330 ha (2016 Census of Agriculture) against 170 farms in 2001, and prepared-food exports grew by about 18,000 t per year since 2000 (+384%), mostly farmed Arctic char plus berries, teas and beverages (pp. 255-258).

outcomes: The US Arctic Fishery Management Plan (2009) and the Central Arctic Ocean Fisheries Agreement (signed 2018; ratified by Canada, the EU, Russia and the US as of August 2019) are described as policy outcomes; no evaluation is given.
findings: The US Arctic Fishery Management Plan (2009, under the Magnuson-Stevens Act) prohibits commercial fishing north of Alaska from the Seward Peninsula to the Canadian border, and the 2018 Central Arctic Ocean Fisheries Agreement covers about 2.8 million km2 with a 16-year limit on commercial fishing and a joint science program that includes Indigenous and local knowledge (pp. 227, 234). || Sub-Arctic Alaska fisheries landed 2.67 million t worth 1.872 billion USD (2010 USD) in 2014, while Alaska prohibits finfish aquaculture (shellfish and kelp earned 1.53 million USD in 2017); in 2018 British Columbia produced 88,834 t of finfish (791 million CAD) and Atlantic Canada 51,634 t (480 million CAD), with no measurable Arctic aquaculture in Canada (pp. 227-228). || Sea-ice extent is falling 3.5-4.1% per decade and precipitation is projected to rise 30-50%; Arctic Cisco from the Mackenzie River (NWT) are carried more than 500 km to Alaskan Beaufort waters, a transboundary freshwater-marine food link supporting subsistence harvests in Utqiaġvik, Nuiqsut and Kaktovik (pp. 229-230). || Recirculating aquaculture systems are proposed as a buffer against climatic extremes but are expensive in capital and operating costs and need high technical expertise (aquaponics is proposed where freshwater is limited), and production at fish farms colder than optimal can rise 11-15% per degree C of warming (Norway evidence) (p. 232).

outcomes: Navahine ended in an agreement with the State of Hawai'i to cut transport greenhouse gas emissions and include children in climate planning (reported through a news source cited in the chapter).
findings: In Navahine v. Hawai'i Department of Transportation, fourteen children and youth sued the State over its transportation system, and the plaintiffs reached an agreement with the State to reduce transport greenhouse gas emissions and include children in climate action plans (p. 45). || In Juliana v. United States, a young plaintiff (Miko) links ocean acidification and warming to the health of marine life and to his own food security (complaint para. 59), and the chapter notes that sea-level rise, coastal erosion and ocean acidification recur in youth climate cases (p. 54).

outcomes: Practitioner-reported case outcomes include Canada's 1,000,000 AF of Columbia River storage for US endangered-species needs, the Catawba-Wateree plan extending yield by 200+ mgd, the 2003 IID-SDCWA transfer, and CALFED's failure to reverse Delta decline; outcomes are not independently evaluated.
findings: A June 2014 workshop in Golden, Colorado (Colorado State University with the US Army Corps of Engineers Institute for Water Resources and the State Department) synthesized 28 US cases and concluded that nexus interactions and success occur mainly at local or basin scale, triggered by a catalyst (crisis, drought, regulatory deadline, relicensing, endangered species) followed by a convening authority, conferred decision authority, a process model and emergent leadership (Executive Summary; Workshop report). || Case summaries present the Columbia River Treaty (Canada stored 1,000,000 AF to help meet US endangered-species needs), Catawba-Wateree relicensing, the Southern Nevada Water Authority, NEWBA and the Navajo Generating Station agreement as arrangements that worked, and CALFED as a program that lost political and financial support before a durable governance structure existed (Workshop report; Cases 3, 18, 21, 25-27). || US baseline (USGS 2005 data): thermoelectric power is 41% and irrigation about 37% of roughly 410,000 Mgal/d of freshwater withdrawals, but irrigation is 80% of consumptive use, and a 40% rise in energy demand could raise energy-sector freshwater demand by 165% (Background paper sect. 1.3, 1.4). || Energy for water varies widely: delivering State Water Project water to San Diego takes 6,900 kWh/AF versus 1,300-3,100 kWh/AF for Central Valley farms, brackish and seawater desalination need 1,400-2,000 and 9,500-38,000 kWh/MG, and water supply and wastewater use about 3% of US city energy and up to 20% in California (Background paper sect. 2.1-2.3). || Aging infrastructure (replacement value exceeding one trillion dollars; capital needs of 632.9 billion USD for water and wastewater over 20 years; projected financing gap of about 27 billion USD per year) makes finance a main driver of the nexus (Workshop report; Background paper sect. 7.3, 8.3); the report gives little attention to equity, Indigenous rights, Alaska or Mexico (evidence-note assessment).

outcomes: The IID-SDCWA transfer was implemented from 2003 with about 30,000 acres per year fallowed; SNWA acquired about 15,000 AF per year of agricultural rights plus leases; a negotiated alternative to the EPA rule for Navajo Generating Station was reached in 2013-2014 (the plant's later closure must be verified).
findings: The 2003 Imperial Irrigation District (IID) to San Diego County Water Authority (SDCWA) agreement, the largest agriculture-to-urban transfer in the US, ramps the transferred volume from 10,000 AF (2003) to almost 200,000 AF (2020) and 200,000 AF per year from 2023 to 2047 (with a provision for a 30-year extension; another case summary gives 45 years renewable for 35), and about 30,000 acres per year are fallowed in IID, mostly alfalfa that would supply southern California dairies (Case 24, pp. 85-88; Case 5). || The transfer's energy effect is conditional: Parker Dam generates about 70 kWh/AF, delivering Colorado River water to SDCWA takes about 1,900 kWh/AF and State Water Project supply about 3,100 kWh/AF, so the transfer saves energy only if it replaces State Water Project water and adds net consumption if it merely augments supply; its energy and food effects had not been studied by 2014 (Case 24). || The Southern Nevada Water Authority acquires agricultural water by purchase and lease (about 15,000 AF/yr owned, about 5,000 AF/yr long-term and about 11,000 AF/yr short-term leases on about 3,500 acres, at 250 falling to 130 USD/AF) for a population projected to grow from 2.06 to 3.18 million by 2050, against a Nevada Colorado River share of 0.3 MAF/yr (Case 26, pp. 93-101). || The Navajo Generating Station (2,250 MW coal) powers Central Arizona Project pumping and supplies revenue to the Navajo and Hopi Tribes; a 2013 EPA NOx rule would require controls costing 544 million USD (possibly over 1.1 billion), and a negotiated alternative retires one unit (or equivalent) in 2020, commits the Interior Department to CO2 cuts of 3% per year (11.3 million t by 2035) and has Reclamation mitigate water-cost impacts (Case 25, pp. 89-92). || Other ag-to-urban fallowing arrangements include Palo Verde Irrigation District to the Metropolitan Water District (25,000-118,000 AF/yr for 35 years, fallowing 7-28% of each landholding) and a 3-year Yuma Mesa pilot (about 9,000 AF/yr from 1,500 acres), with the warning that transfers must not reduce crop yield (Case 5, p. 37).

outcomes: Practitioner-reported results: Geysers pipelines built in 1997 and 2003 added about 170 MW; Austin conserved 700 MW and cut water-utility GHG emissions 85% (2011); Powder River Basin disposition shares measured through 2009.
findings: US oil and gas production generates 15-20 billion bbl of water per year (1.7-2.3 billion gal/d; Argonne 2009), and the Powder River Basin has produced 4.784 billion bbl of coalbed-methane water since 1987 (more than 600,000 AF): 54% was discharged to streams, 35% held in off-channel pits, 5% reused for irrigation, 3% injected and 3% treated and discharged (Case 19, pp. 66-68). || A National Academy of Sciences panel (2010) found that the cost of beneficial use of coalbed-methane produced water almost universally exceeds economic gain under current regulation, and the case concludes that states prioritized energy development over beneficial use of water (Case 19). || At The Geysers, two municipal wastewater pipelines (Southeast Geysers 1997: 9 mgd of secondary effluent, +70 MW; Santa Rosa Geysers 2003: 11 mgd of tertiary effluent, +100 MW, over 200 million USD and 10 years) recharge a 725 MW field with 20 mgd in total and free other water for irrigated vineyards (Case 22, pp. 77-80). || Austin Water uses 210,000 MWh to pump and treat 200 million m3 of water and 100 million m3 of wastewater; Austin Energy has conserved 700 MW and the water utility's 100% wind purchase (2011) cut its GHG emissions 85% (Case 28, p. 106). || The electricity sector accounts for about 35% of US GHG emissions and 41% of withdrawals but 5% of consumptive use, while the water sector accounts for about 13% of US electricity (Case 12, pp. 46-51); Xcel Energy contracts agricultural water (recharge credits, interruptible supply) for thermoelectric cooling, most valuable in droughts, with the water right staying with the farm (Case 20, pp. 69-71).

outcomes: Practitioner-reported: Catawba-Wateree master plan and 2010 interstate settlement; Columbia River storage of 1,000,000 AF for endangered species; CALFED judged underperforming by the Little Hoover Commission and later designated a USDA Critical Conservation Area; 2008 Upper Mississippi flood losses.
findings: The Catawba-Wateree system (Case 18, pp. 62-65) has 11 FERC-licensed reservoirs (built 1904-1963; usable storage 776,747 AF) that supply 18 public water systems (2 million customers) and cool Duke Energy plants totaling 8,591 MW (845 MW hydro, 4,516 MW nuclear, 3,230 MW coal); a plan developed with a 19-member stakeholder team extends water yield by 200+ mgd, moving the modeled yield limit from 2050 to 2100. || The plan was driven by cooperation (a 70-party Comprehensive Relicensing Agreement in 2006), conflict (a South Carolina v. North Carolina Supreme Court case settled in 2010) and climate (droughts of record in 1998-2002 and 2007-2009); an independent facilitator appointed by Duke helped settle the case. || In the Columbia River Treaty (Case 3, pp. 29-31) about 15% of the basin area lies in Canada but about 38% of average flow originates there; the 1964 treaty covers flood-risk management and hydropower, and Canada stored 1,000,000 AF of water to help meet US endangered-species needs, although ecosystem function is not a formal treaty purpose and funding for aging infrastructure is inadequate. || CALFED (Case 21, pp. 72-76), started in 1995 to balance water for food (California has 14.2% of US irrigated acres and half of US fruit and vegetables), cities, energy and ecosystems, improved Delta science and public participation but did not reverse Delta decline or improve supply reliability; the Little Hoover Commission called it costly, underperforming, unfocused and unaccountable, and the case concludes that withdrawing government funding before a durable governance structure exists causes failure. || Inland navigation (Case 14, pp. 53-55) links food and energy transport to water governance: the 2008 Upper Mississippi flood closed the river from 14 June to 5 July and cut tonnage by about 38% (reconstructed from slides), and the International Joint Commission (1912) decides on projects that change transboundary water levels.

outcomes: Field to Market trends measured for 1980-2011; NEWBA demonstrations conducted in 2012-2013; no quantified savings are given for NEWBA.
findings: Field to Market national indicators for corn show irrigation water used per bushel down 53% from 1980 to 2011 and volume per irrigated acre down 28% (16.8 to 12.0 acre-inches), and the slide lists 30% (land), 67% (soil loss), 43% (energy) and 36% (greenhouse gas) per bushel, read here as reductions; gains are attributed to conservation practices, precision farming, better hybrids and biotech (Case 8, pp. 40-42). || Less than 15% of corn acres are irrigated and irrigated corn is under 20% of US irrigated cropland; the 2012 drought cut about 4 billion bushels of production (Case 8). || Ethanol plant metrics for 2012 versus 2008 (column order inferred) are yield 2.82 vs 2.78 gal/bu, thermal energy 23,862 vs 26,206 Btu/gal, electricity 0.75 vs 0.73 kWh/gal and water 2.70 vs 2.72 gal/gal (Case 8, pp. 40-42). || NEWBA (Case 27, pp. 102-105), a voluntary demonstration network of an electric cooperative, vendors and growers (2012-2013) using weather-station evapotranspiration, flow meters cross-checked against power readings, soil-moisture probes and telemetry, found that peer-to-peer demonstrations shorten adoption curves more than traditional research or legislation, that sprinkler package problems and nitrogen movement were greater than expected, and that cost sharing among the energy sector, vendors and growers worked. || Coca-Cola North America (Case 1, pp. 21-24) targets reducing water use 25% and replenishing 100% by 2020 with system agricultural spending above 12.5 billion USD per year and corn as its main US agricultural ingredient, and notes that scaling pilots, misaligned government subsidies and weak public engagement are barriers.

outcomes: By 2018 FID had more than 60 miles of mostly enclosed, gravity-pressurized pipe and 6 screened diversions with in-conduit hydro; MFID had more than 60 miles of buried pipe and a 3.3 MW plant (Low Impact Hydropower Institute certificate in 2018 for two plants); about 98% of FID acreage and about 33-41% of MFID and EFID acreage had converted to on-farm micro-sprinklers by 2016; interviewees describe results as win-win-win and new federal and state laws (2013 hydropower acts, the Conserved Water program) are credited to the pioneers.
findings: Modernization of the Farmers (FID) and Middle Fork (MFID) irrigation districts (piping, pressurization, in-conduit hydropower, horizontal fish screens) eliminated conveyance losses of about 50%, cut FID irrigation water use from 27,000 to 13,000 ac-ft/yr between 1995 and 2013 (33.3 to 16.0 million m3, computed), and let a central pumping station replace more than 1,400 individual pumps, saving about 1.5 million kWh/yr (pp. 51, 73-76). || In-conduit hydropower financed the piping: FID generates about 23.4 million kWh/yr (over 1.9 million USD per year) and MFID about 23 million kWh/yr, hydro was budgeted at 78% of FID revenue in 1986-87, MFID's power revenues covered over 90% of costs most years by 2011, and each district earned about 45 million USD from hydro over 30 years (pp. 74, 79, 110, 136). || FID's hydro (257,386,972 kWh) plus pump savings (18,169,823 kWh) over 2008-2018 equal 504,268,935 lb of CO2 avoided (about 228,700 t) at 1.83 lb/kWh, an emission factor that looks like a marginal fossil rate for a hydro-heavy grid, so the carbon figure is sensitive to factor choice (Table 5, p. 75). || The transition came from economic incentives, fish-protection regulation (Oregon's 1986 One Dead Fish rule; ESA listings of bull trout and steelhead in 1998 and spring Chinook in 1999) and weather disasters (1996 and 2006 floods), enabled by leadership, financial resources, regulations such as PURPA, technology (the patented Farmers Screen), stakeholder relationships and an environmental mindset; seven propositions stress external pressure, lock-in, coordinated action, social learning, risk-taking leadership, community capacity and awareness of interdependence (pp. 93-139, 231-255). || East Fork Irrigation District (EFID) lagged because senior 1895 water rights (106.55 of 117.36 cfs), no federal nexus and no hydro revenue blunted pressure; it diverts 75-85% of late-summer East Fork flow, loses 5,287 ac-ft/yr to end-spills, and a 68.7 million USD modernization plan (NRCS funding about 31 million USD) could save about 4,675 ac-ft/yr by converting the remaining 60% of farms to on-farm upgrades (pp. 191-203).

outcomes: Reports cost over-runs on several recent Canadian reservoir hydro projects and concludes that the decision to complete Site C is justified only by sunk costs (author conclusion from a modeled evaluation).
findings: A purpose-built hourly linear-programming capacity-expansion and dispatch model with balancing-area requirements, wind and solar resources, watershed limits on hydro potential and endogenous electricity trade evaluates the Site C project under construction in British Columbia (abstract). || Modeled: the value of Site C is unlikely to exceed its total cost, and exceeds the avoidable cost of cancellation only where BC and Alberta build additional inter-provincial transmission and pursue 100% decarbonization of their electricity systems (abstract). || Several recent Canadian reservoir hydro projects have had cost over-runs, which can render large hydro uneconomic relative to alternatives; completing Site C is justified only by its high sunk costs (abstract). || The authors present Site C as a cautionary tale for policymakers pursuing large hydroelectric projects (abstract).

outcomes: Identifies cross-domain gains in FEW security from renewable energy in rural Alaska; magnitudes are not reported in the abstract.
findings: In a project on renewable energy in rural Alaska communities, the FEW nexus concept proved a useful framework for identifying cross-domain benefits of renewable energy, including gains in FEW security (abstract). || Transportation and governance also play a major role in determining FEW security outcomes in rural Alaska, beyond what the three domains alone explain (abstract). || The precise configuration of FEW nexus components and their relationships varies by place and time, and the range of factors involved complicates building a functional, systematic FEW model (abstract). || The authors recommend applying the nexus conceptually, to identify cross-domain interactions that matter for long-term sustainability and resilience, rather than as a formal model, and assess how effective the nexus is for describing interactions in rural communities (abstract).

outcomes: Authors state that existing systems, including the Nutrition North subsidy in place since 2011, have not curbed food insecurity: remote fly-in First Nations and Inuit communities eligible for the subsidy still show the highest prevalence in Canada (Discussion, citing Tarasuk et al.).
findings: Of 5,176 participating on-reserve First Nations households, 47.1% were food insecure (95% CI 42.6-51.5): 10.1% marginally, 28.2% moderately and 8.7% severely; regional prevalence ranged from 38.0% to 57.2% (Results, Fig. 1, Table 1). || On-reserve food insecurity is about four times the rate in non-Indigenous Canadian households (48% vs 12%) and above that of off-reserve Indigenous households (27%), as compared in the Discussion with national survey data (Discussion, citing Tarasuk et al.). || Households with children were more food insecure than those without (54% vs 36%); 28.9% of households with children reported child-level food insecurity, and severe food insecurity affected 9% of adults vs 3% of children (Results, Table 1). || Prevalence was higher in Alberta (57.2%, adjusted OR 1.66) and British Columbia (48.6%, adjusted OR 1.91) than in the Atlantic region (Table 2). || Food costs were substantially higher in remote communities, but remoteness was not associated with food insecurity in multivariable analysis; most adults want more traditional food but cite financial and household constraints, industrial activities, regulations, climate change and fear of contamination (abstract).

outcomes: Recommends flushing before use as an interim practice; no program outcome measured.
findings: Stagnant (first-draw) and flushed tap-water samples from 1,516 households in 91 First Nations (11 ecozones) were compared with Health Canada's 2019 Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality (abstract). || Exceedances of the health-based maximum acceptable concentration: lead 8.4% of households (first draw), manganese 4.0%, uranium 1.6%, aluminum 1.3% and copper 0.2% (flushed) (abstract). || Flushing taps cut lead exceedances from 8.4% to 0.7% of households; aluminum exceeded the current operational guidance in 14.2% of households and the proposed guidance in 18.1% (flushed) (abstract). || Aesthetic-objective exceedances (flushed): manganese 12.8%, sodium 5.1%, iron 3.5%, copper 0.4%; taste and color were the main reasons households limited tap-water use (abstract). || The authors judge trace-metal quality satisfactory overall but find elevated lead in some communities and recommend flushing taps before use until action can be taken (abstract).

outcomes: Documents the historical outcome that Diné water claims were denied while Phoenix and Tucson gained Colorado River water through the Central Arizona Project; recent Arizona-Navajo Nation settlements are read as continuing that pattern (qualitative archival analysis).
findings: Archival documents are used to trace the colonial politics behind bringing Colorado River water into Phoenix and Tucson (abstract). || The 1922 Colorado River Compact, Arizona's 1960s Central Arizona Project campaign and recent Indian water settlements between Arizona and the Navajo Nation enlarged Arizona's population and power while denying Diné water claims (abstract). || The resulting infrastructures formed a coal-energy-water nexus that relied on Navajo coal while building Arizona's water network (abstract). || The author argues that such projects work as colonial beachheads, encroaching on Indigenous lands and livelihoods and widening inequalities over time (abstract).

outcomes: Yields lessons for engagement design; no quantified project outcomes are reported.
findings: Authors reflect on their experience engaging Anishinaabe Tribal Nations in the Great Lakes region to support Tribal sovereignty in food, energy and water (FEW) decision-making (abstract). || Tribal Nations bring a deep commitment to sovereignty and cultural strengths but are challenged by shortages of administrative capacity and technical support and by economic, socio-cultural and institutional dynamics that limit enacting that sovereignty (abstract). || Engagement by university professionals is often mismatched with Tribal priorities, and partnerships struggle when university partners do not acknowledge these realities (abstract). || Effective engagement requires practical knowledge, applied assistance and genuine relationships, which run counter to the structures and priorities of universities, federal funding agencies and student recruitment (abstract).

outcomes: Observed pattern across 194 projects: rising equity ownership but limited control, and little involvement of Metis and Inuit communities; the authors link better outcomes to equity ownership, FPIC and policy supports.
findings: A community-energy framework was used to characterize and analyze 194 renewable energy projects associated with Indigenous communities in Canada by legal form, project location and control (abstract). || The findings do not provide strong indications of reconciliation (abstract). || Equity ownership has risen over time, but most projects on traditional territories and in Indigenous communities have minority or no Indigenous ownership (abstract). || No projects are associated with Metis communities and only 6 with Inuit communities; 41 projects are controlled by Indigenous communities (abstract). || Institutional change requires free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) and extensive policy supports (abstract).

outcomes: The 2011 switch from Food Mail to Nutrition North Canada is estimated to have increased food insecurity (8.9 percentage points overall; 7.3 percentage points severe among Indigenous families), most in the territories and Inuit Nunangat and where children were present (observed, quasi-experimental).
findings: Food insecurity is prevalent in northern Canada, especially among Indigenous peoples; the federal government subsidizes shipping of necessities to remote northern communities, first through the Food Mail Program and, from April 2011, through Nutrition North Canada (abstract). || A difference-in-differences model on Canadian Community Health Survey data (2007-2016), robust to several checks, finds the policy change raised the likelihood of overall food insecurity by 8.9 percentage points (77.3% relative to the sample mean) and of moderate or severe food insecurity by 7.1 percentage points (89.3%) (abstract). || Severe food insecurity among Indigenous families rose by 7.3 percentage points, more than three times the sample mean (abstract). || Effects varied by region and subsample: the change was particularly harmful to Indigenous families in the territories and Inuit Nunangat, and the harm was heightened where children were present (abstract).

outcomes: Ex post test of the existing Tarifa 09 energy-quota rule: it did not constrain extraction in the sampled orchards. No change to the formula is reported; the authors propose a volume-based limit (Discussion, pp. 413-414).
findings: The energy quota that caps subsidized electricity for agricultural pumping (the Tarifa 09 stimulus tariff) follows a formula changed by a 2005 agreement, Energy Quota = 438 + HP x 4,901.22 kWh per year, which removed the granted water volume as a variable so that the quota depends only on pump horsepower (Introduction, p. 398; Methodology, p. 406). || Annual electricity use of 195 subsidized services in Linares and Hualahuises (CFE bills supplied by beneficiaries, November 2023) was significantly lower than their assigned quotas (Mann-Whitney W = 33,193, p < 2.2e-16), so the quota does not limit pumping effectively (Methodology, p. 402; Results, p. 408). || Flow meters inspected in three citrus orchards with surface irrigation (November 2022) showed extraction of 1.46, 1.30 and 11.48 hm3 per year against granted volumes of 0.040, 0.117 and 1.045 hm3 per year, i.e., about 36, 11 and 11 times the granted volume; only 8.4% of the 14.25 hm3 extracted was within the granted volume (Results, p. 407, Table 1; Discussion, p. 411). || Two of the three orchards stayed below their energy quota (189,600 of 637,596 kWh; 209,310 of 355,776 kWh) while over-pumping, and the third exceeded its quota by 14% (711,069 vs 622,892 kWh) (Results, p. 407, Table 1). || The abstract reports an excess extraction of 13.047 hm3, equal to 17.4% of the annual recharge of the Citrícola Sur aquifer (75.1 hm3), an aquifer under an extraction ban since April 2013 whose CONAGUA availability is a deficit of -88.86 hm3 per year (abstract; Methodology, p. 402; Discussion, p. 410).

outcomes: State emergency declaration (2022) and a Ministry of Social Policy-led response (tankers, tanks, cisterns, bottled water); improved distribution in informal settlements; the authors identify the absence of a preparedness plan as the main gap (abstract).
findings: In 2022 Nuevo León declared a state of emergency: precipitation fell to about 400 mm, the Cerro Prieto reservoir dropped to 1% of capacity between June and October 2022, and a 19 June 2022 aqueduct fissure left 40-50% of the population without water for two days (full text, 'The context of a water scarcity climate emergency'). || Emergency actions were financed with 2,196 million MXN (about 115 million USD): 58.4% from the state water utility SADM, 40.1% from other state agencies and 1.6% federal; 45% went to deep wells, 19% to water trucks and community cisterns, 15% to pressure-regulating valves, 12% to shallow wells, 4% to interconnection with irrigation channels and 2% to dam pumping (full text, Findings, 'Elements of a subnational emergency response'). || The Ministry of Social Policy response delivered more than 3,000 household tanks (250 L), more than 500 community cisterns (5,000 and 10,000 L), 400 hydration points and about 950,000 bottles of water; before the emergency 14.3% of Nuevo León households had no tank to store water and 154 informal settlements lacked basic services (full text, Context; Findings, 'Elements of a subnational emergency response'). || Facilitators were the emergency declaration as a policy instrument, multi- and inter-sectoral collaboration, pre-existing social and data infrastructure, technical capacity to identify low-income households without water and flexibility to convert regular activities; challenges were citizen discontent, no preparedness plan, scarce household storage, initial inefficiencies with tanker distribution, steep terrain for cisterns and staff burnout (abstract). || Private companies agreed with the federal government to cede part of their industrial well-water rights to complement the human-consumption supply, and the response improved water distribution in informal settlements as a positive externality (full text, Findings, Implementation outcomes, Adoption; abstract).

outcomes: Real-world effect of an existing treatment step: lower predicted bacterial infection risk in the treated canal system, no reduction for Giardia or viruses, and loss of the benefit after the sentinel community (abstract).
findings: Urban wastewater reuse in agriculture provides reliable, nutrient-rich water, reduces water stress and strengthens food systems, but carries health risks; the study compares treated vs untreated wastewater and upstream vs downstream of communities in Mezquital Valley irrigation canals (abstract). || Treatment reduced predicted bacterial infection risk at post-treatment sampling points (RR = 0.73, 95% CI 0.61-0.87), with no evidence of similar reductions for Giardia (RR = 1.02, 95% CI 0.56-1.86) or viral pathogens (RR = 1.18, 95% CI 0.70-2.02) (abstract). || Infection risk decreased further down the canals but rose for bacterial pathogens after the sentinel community (RR = 1.94, 95% CI 1.34-2.86), and the benefits of treatment were lost after the community: in the comparison of the treated section with a canal section carrying untreated wastewater the reported RRs were 5.27 vs 2.08 for bacteria and 6.98 vs 3.35 for Giardia, before vs after the sentinel community (abstract). || The authors attribute the increase in risk after transit through communities to local recontamination of the treated wastewater stream (abstract).

outcomes: Binding federal water program for 2026-2030 (published in the DOF on 18 May 2026), aligned with the 2024 National Agreement for the Human Right to Water and Sustainability (DOF 19 Dec 2024) and the December 2025 reform of water law; implementation outcomes are not yet reported (irrigation indicator baseline 0 in 2024).
findings: In 2023, of the groundwater extracted from Mexico's 653 aquifers, 71.1% went to agriculture, 20.9% to public supply, 6.9% to industry and 1.1% to thermoelectric generation; 286 aquifers have no groundwater availability (PDF pp. 8-9). Groundwater is 39.9% (36,165 hm3) of consumptive concessions and groundwater concessions equal almost one third of recharge (p. 8). || Total concessioned volume was 267,350.06 hm3 in December 2023, of which 90,629.48 hm3 consumptive and 176,711.12 hm3 for hydropower (non-consumptive) (p. 12). || Irrigated agriculture consumes 76.3% of concessioned water at an efficiency of 33-55%, gravity systems predominate, groundwater irrigates 2.6 Mha (about one third of the irrigated area) and 31.9% of collected municipal wastewater is untreated (p. 22; 143.8 of 211.2 m3/s treated in 2024, 68.1% coverage, p. 14). || Objective 3 sets a national irrigation-technification program for 200,000 ha in 13 priority districts (indicator 3.1: baseline 0 in 2024; targets 9.95% in 2026, 18.97% in 2027, 29.47% in 2028, 59.47% in 2029, 100% in 2030), crop conversion according to sustainable availability (line 3.1.4), voluntary return of unused agricultural and industrial rights, and a review of more than 500,000 concession titles (pp. 27, 29, 37, 45-46). || Energy enters the program only through line of action 2.2.3 (CONAGUA with CFE) on energy efficiency of electromechanical systems and renewables in water, sewerage and sanitation services (p. 36) and a line on solar-powered purification for community systems (p. 37); a full-text search finds no line of action on agricultural electricity tariffs or pumping subsidies ('bombeo' has no match; 'tarifa' appears once, for water-service tariffs, p. 21) and the word 'nexo' does not occur.

outcomes: Accounting shows Lower Basin consumption fell 2000-2019 (municipal, commercial and industrial -38%; agriculture -15%) while agreements were adopted; all agreements except the 2001 Interim Surplus Guidelines expire in 2026 (Introduction).
findings: Averaged over 2000-2019, irrigated agriculture accounted for 74% of direct human uses and 52% of overall consumption of Colorado River water, and water consumed for agriculture was three times all other direct uses combined (abstract). || Cattle-feed crops (alfalfa and other grass hays) accounted for 46% of direct consumption, 32% of all water consumed and 62% of agricultural consumption (abstract; Results, Table 1). || An average of 23.7 billion m3 (19.3 million acre-feet) per year was consumed before the river reached its delta; riparian and wetland evapotranspiration took 19% and reservoir evaporation 11%, and 47 inter-basin transfer systems exported about 12% of the river's water, so nearly 19% of the river's water is exported or used in Mexico (Introduction; Results; Discussion). || In Mexico, irrigated crops account for 86% of direct human uses and 80% of total water consumed, the highest crop share of any accounting unit (Results, Tables 1-2). || Between 2000 and 2019 consumption in the Lower Basin fell by 38% in the municipal, commercial and industrial sector and by 15% in agriculture, which the authors attribute in part to mandated reductions under the 2007 Guidelines, Minutes 319 and 323 and the 2019 Drought Contingency Plans (Results; Introduction).

outcomes: Drought Response Operations Agreement under the Upper Basin DCP targets Lake Powell protection at 3,525 ft; Reclamation is considering structural and operational changes at Glen Canyon Dam and Congress is asked to weigh financial relief for power customers (pp. 9-10, 15-17).
findings: Glen Canyon Power Plant has 1,320 MW of nameplate capacity (eight generators), but low head at low reservoir levels had reduced its capacity to about 59% of nameplate, or 778 MW, in early 2023 (Hydropower Generation and Marketing, pp. 6-7). || Minimum power pool is 1,064 m (3,490 ft), 6 m (20 ft) above the penstocks; on 11 March 2023 Lake Powell stood at 1,073 m (3,520 ft), its lowest on record, 9.4 m (31 ft) above minimum power pool and below Reclamation's 1,074 m (3,525 ft) protection target under the Drought Response Operations Agreement (pp. 5, 9-11). || Glen Canyon accounts for 73% of the generation capacity of WAPA's Salt Lake City Area/Integrated Projects and historically 65-75% of its generation; power is sold at cost to 130 wholesale customers serving about 5 million people and 53 Tribal Nations, and low-cost 'project use power' supports pumping for Upper Basin irrigation districts (p. 7). || If Lake Powell fell below minimum power pool the river outlets (425 m3/s, 15,000 cfs) could pass up to 13,445 million m3 (10.9 MAF) per year, but at 1,045 m (3,430 ft) discharge capacity would be about 289 m3/s (10,200 cfs), or 9,140 million m3 (7.41 MAF) per year, below the 10,152 million m3 (8.23 MAF) per year Law of the River requirement; below 1,027 m (3,370 ft) about 2,331 million m3 (1.89 MAF) would remain as dead storage (p. 13). || Low Glen Canyon output raises costs unevenly for WAPA customers (the Navajo Tribal Utility Authority buys about 7% of WAPA supply, which is about 42% of its own supply; Tri-State takes 23% of WAPA sales but about 8% of its supply), displaces hydropower with fossil generation (higher greenhouse gas emissions) and threatens Upper Colorado River Basin Fund balances that also support project irrigators (pp. 13-15).

outcomes: Documents the reversal of electricity flows under 2023 low-precipitation conditions; no policy outcome.
findings: After two years of abnormally low precipitation across Canada, Quebec exports to the US fell to 13.3 TWh in 2023 from 25.9 TWh in 2019 (about -49%, computed), while British Columbia imports from the US Pacific Northwest rose to 16.8 TWh from 11.2 TWh (opening paragraph, Figure 1). || In 2023 B.C. generated 56.1 TWh and was a net importer of 10.2 TWh (18% of its production); Quebec generated 195.6 TWh and net-exported 12.1 TWh (6%); Ontario generated 156.3 TWh and net-exported 13.5 TWh (9%); Manitoba generated 33.3 TWh and net-exported 5.2 TWh (16%) (text under Figure 1). || Installed hydroelectric capacity is largest in Quebec (41 GW), B.C. (16 GW), Ontario (9 GW), Newfoundland and Labrador (8 GW) and Manitoba (6 GW); surplus is sold into US Northeast and Midcontinent markets, but Canadian exports are a fraction of the receiving US demand ('Big Hydro Producers in Canada'). || Quebec paid an average of $78.49 per MWh for US imports in 2019-2023 against $47.81 per MWh received for exports (Ontario 2019-2024: $57.15 vs $41.77), and B.C.'s reservoir hydro lets it conserve water for high-demand periods while importing cheaper US power ('Recent Electricity Price Trends').

outcomes: Observed outcomes: farmland contraction on the US side lowered consumption, irrigation in Mexico expanded, basin-wide consumption stayed high, and Mexico's treaty deliveries lagged (debt 1,280 MCM at end of 2024).
findings: Accounting of 14 sub-basins for 2000-2019 shows irrigated agriculture is 87% of direct consumption and nearly seven times all other direct uses combined; cattle-feed crops are 56% of irrigation water, and municipal and commercial use is only 7% of direct consumption (sects. 2.2, 4). || Indirect uses are 56% of overall consumption: riparian evapotranspiration 44% and reservoir evaporation 12% (sect. 2.4). || Since 2002 depletion has averaged about 2,900 MCM/yr (reservoirs 177.6, aquifers 2,700, river outflow 22.4 MCM/yr), so 52% of direct consumption is unsustainable; overconsumption exceeds direct consumption in the Pecos sub-basin (140%) and reaches 85% in Rio Grande New Mexico (sects. 3.1-3.4; abstract). || Direct consumption rose by 12.1 MCM per year: US-side use fell by 43.1 MCM/yr as irrigated farmland contracted (farmland loss of 18% in the Colorado headwaters, 36% in New Mexico and 49% on the Pecos), while Mexican use rose by 55.2 MCM/yr (sect. 2.3; abstract). || At the end of 2024 reservoirs held 26% of capacity (Rio Conchos 20%, New Mexico Rio Grande 13%), Mexico's 1944-Treaty water debt stood at 1,280 MCM and Texas lower-valley farmers lost nearly 500 million USD in 2024; even if cities and power plants stopped using water, over-consumption would fall by only 25% (sect. 4).

outcomes: Minute 330 (2024) created a 2023-2026 Mexican conservation program; Minute 334 (signed 2 Sep 2026) extends and replaces Minutes 323 and 330 through 2028, cuts deliveries to Mexico by 308.4 million m3 (250,000 acre-feet) a year in 2027-2028 and adds a Salinity Pilot Program for 2027-2028 (IBWC, 9 Sep 2026).
findings: In 2024 the US and Mexico signed Minute 330, under which Mexico committed to create additional water savings through 2026, complementing conservation by the US Lower Basin states (abstract). || The study uses semi-structured interviews with members of the Minute Negotiating Group from both countries and with experts from federal water agencies, NGOs, universities, US state water agencies and Mexican water-user leaders to examine the motivations, negotiation and implementation of Minute 330 (abstract). || Minute 330 responded to scarcity challenges that prior minutes could not address, and it set an important precedent for cooperation and cross-border collaboration between the two countries under unprecedented circumstances (abstract). || The authors argue these features matter for the post-2026 process and for new regulations to manage the Colorado River at binational and US national scales (abstract).

outcomes: The Great Lakes Compact (2008) has kept diversions out of the basin apart from the Waukesha exemption; renegotiation of the Colorado River Compact is being called for amid aridification (authors' assessment).
findings: The 1922 Colorado River Compact, the 1938 Rio Grande Compact and the 1944 Water Treaty allocate extractions of a limited resource, whereas the 2008 Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Compact restricts diversions from a basin with variable but relatively abundant supplies (sect. 'Contrasting continental compacts'). || A continental gradient is opening: Colorado and Rio Grande flows keep declining while Lake Michigan-Huron rose to record highs in 2017-2020; the Ogallala aquifer declines without any multi-jurisdictional agreement, Joliet (Illinois) moved its supply from the depleted Cambrian-Ordovician aquifer to Lake Michigan, and Waukesha (Wisconsin) obtained a recently approved exemption from the Compact's diversion ban because of naturally occurring radium in its groundwater (Introduction; sect. 'Contrasting continental compacts'). || The 1944 Treaty has no third party to reconcile disputes and a US-Mexico power imbalance limits the capacity of the Minute process to accommodate shrinking supplies, whereas the Colorado Compact relies on the US government as arbiter; the Great Lakes Compact has been immune to outside demand except Waukesha, which the authors credit to its careful wording and regional political stability (sect. 'Linkages between compact failure, climate change, and management'). || The authors recommend a summit of compact and treaty leaders to assess vulnerabilities, a review of the US Supreme Court decision in Texas v. New Mexico and Colorado, and attention to whether treaties in water-rich regions will 'hold water' through mid-century (sect. 'Moving forward').

outcomes: Interim measures have been implemented since November 2024 (3.6 MAF Arrow Lakes flood storage, Entitlement reduced 37%, Powerex taking over transmission rights); the modernized treaty text had not been released as of 3 December 2024 and needs Senate advice and consent.
findings: The 1961 Treaty provided 19,119 million m3 (15.5 MAF) of additional storage in Canada through four dams (three in Canada, one in the US) for flood control and hydropower; in exchange the US pays lump sums and gives Canada a share of downstream hydropower benefits (the Canadian Entitlement), estimated at up to 335 million USD a year (Summary; Introduction, p. 1). || The July 2024 agreement in principle keeps 4,441 million m3 (3.6 MAF) per year of preplanned flood storage behind Keenleyside Dam for 37.6 million USD per year (indexed) through 2044 from spring 2025, plus 16.6 million USD per year once the agreement enters into force (p. 12). || The Canadian Entitlement falls about 37% from August 2024 and about 50% by 2033: capacity from 1,141 MW (2024) to 660 MW (2025-2029) and 550 MW (2034-2044), and generation from 454 to 305 to 225 (reported as 'Generation (Megawatts)'); it falls a further 6.5% for each MAF of reduced coordinated storage, down to 14,185 million m3 (11.5 MAF) through 2039 and 12,952 million m3 (10.5 MAF) through 2044 (pp. 12-13, Table 1). || Canada keeps releasing 1,233 million m3 (1 MAF) per year from its reservoirs for salmon migration with a new additional 617 million m3 (0.5 MAF) in dry years, and a Tribal and Indigenous-led body would advise on ecosystem needs; critics note the agreement lacks an 'ecosystem function' purpose and prioritizes hydropower and flood control (pp. 13-14). || Interim measures announced 25 November 2024: Canada provides 4,441 million m3 (3.6 MAF) per year at Arrow Lakes for 2024-2027 if the US elects and pays; the Entitlement decreased 37% from 1 August 2024; and from 1 November 2024 Powerex assumed, and pays for, 1,120 MW of BPA transmission rights; changes to the treaty text would need Senate advice and consent (p. 14; Summary).

outcomes: Observed outcomes: the 2020-2025 Rio Grande cycle closed at 0.88 of 1.75 MAF; Mexico committed in February 2026 to at least 432 million m3 (0.35 MAF) per year and a repayment plan; the US denied a Tijuana Colorado River delivery in March 2025; Minute 333 on Tijuana sanitation was agreed on 15 December 2025.
findings: Under the 1944 Treaty Mexico must deliver one-third of the flow of specified tributaries, at least 432 million m3 (0.35 MAF) per year on average over five-year cycles, i.e., 2,159 million m3 (1.75 MAF) per cycle; at the end of the 2020-2025 cycle in late October 2025 Mexico had delivered 1,085 million m3 (0.88 MAF) according to IBWC, and Mexico has missed cycle obligations on multiple occasions since 1994 (Rio Grande section). || In February 2026 the State Department announced that Mexico committed to annual deliveries of at least 432 million m3 (0.35 MAF) and to a plan to address the 2020-2025 shortfall; the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 conditions some funds on certification of Mexican deliveries (Rio Grande section). || In March 2025 the US denied, for the first time in the treaty's history, Mexico's request to deliver Colorado River water to Tijuana (average diversion 2.07 million m3 (1,678 acre-feet) per year in 2020-2024, authorized through 2027 under Minute 327); bills S. 3120 and H.R. 6386 would link Rio Grande deliveries to Colorado River delivery requests (Colorado River; Congressional Considerations). || Tijuana River Valley sanitation: Minute 328 (2022) commits 144 million USD from Mexico and 330 million USD from the US, and Minute 333 (15 December 2025) sets up a binational work group and requires Mexico to build a new treatment plant in Tijuana; US appropriations include 156.1 million USD for the IBWC Construction account (FY2024) and 250 million USD in supplemental appropriations to IBWC (FY2025) (Tijuana River Valley section). || Stakeholders cite drought in Mexico's Rio Grande basin and weather and climate patterns, in addition to Mexico's internal water management, as drivers of delivery shortfalls, and a 2022 IBWC-commissioned white paper lists desalination, conservation and storage projects in Texas and Mexico as ways to expand supply; some Members of Congress want the treaty addressed in the USMCA review (Rio Grande; Congressional Considerations).

outcomes: Observed depletion kept accelerating during the early years of SGMA implementation (8.58 km3/yr in 2019-2021), which the authors use to argue for expedited implementation; no SGMA effect is measured.
findings: NASA GRACE and GRACE-FO observations show Central Valley groundwater depletion accelerating: 1.86 km3/yr over 1961-2021, 2.41 km3/yr over 2003-2021 and 8.58 km3/yr over 2019-2021, a period of megadrought in southwestern North America (abstract). || Loss rates in the three droughts were 6.59 km3/yr in 2006-2011 (30.2 km3 lost), 6.56 km3/yr in 2011-2017 (37.1 km3 lost, more than the 32.2 km3 capacity of Lake Mead) and 8.58 km3/yr from September 2019 to December 2021 (20.0 km3 lost), about 31% faster than the two earlier droughts and nearly five times the long-term rate (Results, Table 1). || Surface-water cuts drive pumping: in 12 of the 18 years studied the State Water Project or Central Valley Project allocation fell below 50%, contributing to 1.4 Lake Mead volumes of groundwater loss; allocations of 0% (CVP, 2014-2015) and 5% (SWP, 2014) coincided with annual losses of 9.66 and 7.64 km3 in 2014 and 2015, and 2021 matched the 2014 record of 9.22 km3 (Results, Fig. 5). || The Tulare basin lost 15.1 km3 in 2003-2021, nearly 40% of the Valley total, from about one quarter of the area (Results, Table 2). || The Central Valley supplies an estimated 25% of US food consumption (US$17 billion per year) and gets two thirds or more of irrigation water from groundwater in drought, while SGMA is being implemented slowly over 27 years from 2015 (abstract, Introduction).

outcomes: Observed outcome of LEPA adoption across the Kansas High Plains Aquifer 1994-2016: no reduction in pumping, energy use -19.2% and GHG -15.2%, but rising pumping lift offset the gains.
findings: Across the Kansas High Plains Aquifer from 1994 to 2016, widespread adoption of low-energy precision application (LEPA) and related low-pressure irrigation technologies did not slow pumping but reduced irrigation energy use by 19.2% and GHG emissions by 15.2% (abstract). || Water-level declines offset the efficiency gains: deeper water tables quadrupled the share of GHG emissions from direct on-site fuel combustion, offsetting the decarbonization of the regional electricity grid (abstract). || The authors conclude that adopting low-pressure irrigation technology, absent policies that incentivize or mandate reduced water use, ultimately increases the energy and carbon footprints of irrigated agriculture (abstract). || Method: annual 1994-2016 estimates combine detailed water use, irrigation type and pump energy source data with aquifer water-level and groundwater chemistry data and life cycle assessment (abstract).

outcomes: Earliest Kansas LEMA, 2013-2017: water use 31% below control scenarios; 72% of savings from irrigation efficiency and 19% from crop switching; irrigated area largely maintained; groundwater levels showing early stabilization.
findings: Kansas created the Local Enhanced Management Area (LEMA) program in 2012, empowering farmers to work with local and state officials on five-year, enforceable groundwater conservation programs; a causal-impact analysis (Bayesian structural time series) of the earliest LEMA over 2013-2017 found water use 31% lower than control scenarios, with early signs of stabilizing groundwater levels (abstract). || Of the savings, 72% came from improved irrigation efficiency (less water applied to existing crops) and 19% from expansion of crops with lower water demand, while farmers largely maintained irrigated area (abstract). || Satellite-derived irrigated area and crop-type maps were combined with well records to partition savings among reduced area, reduced application and crop switching (abstract). || The authors conclude that irrigator-driven conservation programs with regulatory oversight can provide a path to sustainability in stressed aquifers (abstract).

outcomes: Documents what happened on 925 installed arrays by 2018: cropland and crops displaced, fallowing of adjacent irrigated land at 58 utility-scale sites, and installation timing relative to SGMA; lifespan food, water and economic effects are modeled.
findings: 925 agrisolar arrays (2.53 GWp on 3,930 ha, installed 2008-2018) replaced about 0.10% of Central Valley active farmland; over a 25-year lifespan they displace about 1.57 Tkcal of food (0.16 Tkcal from commercial-scale and 1.41 Tkcal from utility-scale arrays), 58% of the commercial-scale loss being grain (abstract; Results, offset food production). || Water: 74% of arrays replaced irrigated cropland, cutting water use by 5.46 thousand m3/ha/yr (commercial-scale) and 6.02 thousand m3/ha/yr (utility-scale), totaling 42.1 million m3 and 544 million m3 over 25 years (Results, changes in water use). || Economics: commercial-scale landowners' lifetime net footprint is about US$124,000/ha/yr, 25 times the lost food revenue (US$4,920/ha/yr), driven by net metering and offset electricity costs; utility-scale landowners net only US$2,690/ha/yr (46 times less) and the worst-case budget is negative (-US$432/ha/yr) (Results, economic footprint). || Energy: cumulative generation by 2042 is projected at 10 TWh (commercial-scale) and 113 TWh (utility-scale), with 11 GWh and 146 GWh of irrigation electricity avoided (Results). || Adjacent irrigated cropland was fallowed at 58 utility-scale installations (658 MWp, 968 ha, 27% of utility-scale area), suggesting an emergent 'solar fallowing' practice; 46% of utility-scale and 58% of commercial-scale arrays were completed after SGMA was enacted (Discussion).

outcomes: National outcome 2008-2020: thermoelectric withdrawals fell by 14,335 million L/day and consumption by 278 million L/day, attributed mainly to coal replacement and the decline of once-through cooling.
findings: Across the conterminous US, thermoelectric (TE) plant water withdrawal and consumption trends declined by 14,335 and 278 million L/day, respectively, over 2008-2020 (abstract). || The declines are driven largely by the switch from coal-fired plants to other generation technologies; once-through cooling shows large declining trends while recirculating tower cooling shows small increasing consumption trends (abstract). || Fifteen hydrologic regions show decreasing trends in withdrawals and consumption; the largest decreases are at coal plants with once-through freshwater cooling in the Great Lakes and Ohio regions, whereas natural gas combined cycle plants with recirculating towers show increasing consumption in most regions (abstract). || Some plants with tower or once-through cooling withdraw, on average, volumes close to or above average simulated streamflow, mostly in the central and eastern US, which could cause water availability problems, thermal pollution of ecosystems and generation constraints (abstract).

outcomes: Real retrofits 2013-2022: NGCC replacement sharply and persistently reduced per-MWh water withdrawal, discharge and carbon; boiler conversions did not.
findings: Thermoelectric plants account for about 40% of US water withdrawals; in 2022, 48.5 trillion gallons (about 184 billion m3) were withdrawn for cooling and 962.9 billion gallons (about 3.6 billion m3) consumed, and coal steam plants withdrew 18.3 trillion gallons (about 69 billion m3) while producing 19.7% of net generation (abstract). || An event study of the 2013-2022 retrofits (17 coal plants replaced by natural gas combined cycle, NGCC, and 167 coal steam units at 85 plants converted to burn gas) finds that replacement by NGCC cut water withdrawal by 40.2-53.9 thousand gallons per MWh (about 152-204 m3/MWh), discharge by 30.7 thousand gallons per MWh (about 116 m3/MWh) and carbon emissions by 0.59 short tons per MWh (about 0.54 t/MWh) (abstract). || Boiler conversion produced no statistically significant change in per-MWh withdrawal, consumption, discharge or carbon emissions (abstract). || 204.6 GW of coal-fired capacity remained operable in 2022, so fuel transition should account for water-stressed regions and treat water and electricity as interdependent (abstract).

outcomes: Observed fleet outcome 1980-2022: capacity factors fell at most plants, a net 13% generation loss even after upgrades.
findings: Annual capacity factor declined at about four fifths of US hydropower plants (482 of 610 plants above 5 MW) between 1980 and 2022; 318 of the declines are significant at p < 0.05 (about thirteen times as many significant decreases as increases), and the median trend is -2.6 percentage points per decade (abstract; Results). || Fleetwide, the capacity factor trend implies a 23% cumulative generation decrease since 1980 (about 14.5 TWh per decade), equivalent to retiring a Hoover Dam (3.6 TWh/yr) every two to three years; the actual net loss is 13% (8.2 TWh per decade) because more than half of plants added capacity (Results). || Water availability explains the decline at only 21% of plants (62 of 288 modeled plants with a negative trend have at least 60% of the trend explained by water), and 117 of 362 modeled plants (one third) show declining capacity factors despite increasing water availability, pointing to equipment deterioration and dam operations for non-power objectives (abstract; Results). || In the Pacific Northwest, where hydropower supplies about two thirds of generation, the implied loss is 6.2 TWh per decade (just over 5% of regional hydropower output); all ten plants above 1,000 MW show negative trends (Results).

outcomes: Realized RFS effects 2008-2016: corn price +31%, corn area +2.8 Mha, cropland +2.1 Mha, fertilizer use +3-8%, water quality degradants +3-5%, and no GHG benefit for corn ethanol relative to gasoline.
findings: The Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) raised corn prices by about 30% (31%, 95% CI 5-70%) and other crop prices by about 20%, expanding US corn cultivation by 2.8 Mha (8.7%) and total cropland by 2.1 Mha (2.4%) over 2008-2016 (abstract; Results). || These changes increased national fertilizer use by 3-8% (reactive nitrogen +7.5%), nitrate leaching by 5.3%, phosphorus runoff by 3.2% and soil erosion by 4.7%, and raised N2O emissions by 8.3% (4.1 Tg CO2e/yr) (abstract; Results). || Land-use change emissions of 397.7 Tg CO2e (2008-2016) imply 29.7 g CO2e/MJ for corn ethanol (38.7 including N2O); substituting this for the EPA's modeled domestic value raises ethanol's projected 2022 life-cycle intensity to 115.7 g CO2e/MJ, 24% above gasoline (93.1), so the RFS corn ethanol is no less carbon intensive than gasoline (Results). || The RFS stimulated 20.8 billion L (5.5 billion gal) of added annual ethanol, using nearly 1.3 billion bushels of corn; each additional billion gallons of annual ethanol demand implies +5.6% corn price, +1.6% corn area and +0.4% cropland (Results).

outcomes: Observed land-cover outcomes at solar and wind sites 2009-2020: most sites stay in agricultural land cover, but solar sites on continuous cropland are often fallowed and 15% of solar sites leave agriculture.
findings: In 2020 the land directly affected by rural utility-scale solar and wind farms was small relative to about 897 million acres (363 Mha) of farmland: an estimated 336,000 acres (136,000 ha) for solar and 88,000 acres (35,600 ha) for wind (Summary, What Did the Study Find?). || Before development, solar farms sat on cropland (43%), pasture-rangeland (21%) and nonagricultural land (17%), while wind turbines sat on cropland (56%) and pasture-rangeland (36%); in the Midwest 66% of solar sites and 93% of wind sites were cropland, whereas most Plains and West solar sites were pasture-rangeland (60% and 51%) (Summary). || Land cover changed within three years before to three years after installation at 26% of solar sites but only 5% of wind sites; 15% of solar sites shifted out of agriculture (under 1% for wind), and 36% of solar sites on continuous cropland were fallow in at least one of the three post-installation years vs 7% for wind (Summary). || Most cropland sites stayed in the same land-cover class after installation (82% for solar, 99% for wind), and the average annual rate of land-cover change was largely unchanged after development (Summary).

outcomes: Evaluates 108 submitted plans; 'outcomes' are the protection that plan thresholds would give to wells and ecosystems, not measured groundwater changes.
findings: The study scored 108 SGMA Groundwater Sustainability Plans (162,943 pages of text) on four components (engage, describe, analyze, act) for agriculture, domestic and environmental stakeholders: 91% of plans did not comprehensively integrate stakeholders, and only 9% scored above zero on every component for every group (Results, incomplete and variable stakeholder integration). || Plan thresholds leave most users unprotected: 60% of agricultural wells, 63% of domestic wells and 91% of groundwater-dependent ecosystems fall below the protection offered by the plans' minimum thresholds; 40% of agricultural wells (14,964), 37% of domestic wells (32,449) and 9% of ecosystem area (138 km2) were protected (abstract; Results, most wells and ecosystems are not protected). || Higher stakeholder integration goes with better protection for domestic wells (mean 25.9% protected at low integration vs 46.6% at high, p <= 0.001) and ecosystems (6.3% vs 18.7%, p <= 0.01), but not for agriculture (40.8% vs 48.2%, not significant) (Results). || Only 24% of plans set minimum thresholds specifically to protect wells or ecosystems; 76% used non-stakeholder approaches such as lowest historical levels, and economically vulnerable subgroups are less integrated and, where data allow, less protected (Results).

outcomes: Prospective evaluation of thresholds proposed in 60 plans; no realized outcomes are measured.
findings: In all 35 Central Valley subbasins studied, plans set some minimum thresholds (MTs) below 2019 groundwater levels; on average MTs are nearly 24 m (80 ft) deeper than 2019 levels and 23 of 60 plans (13 subbasins) set over 150 MTs (11%) more than 61 m (200 ft) below 2019 levels (Results). || The MTs resemble business-as-usual decline; if groundwater reaches them, about 30% of drinking water wells would be partially or fully dewatered: 32% of domestic wells (n = 9,285) and 21% of public supply wells (n = 1,168), with 18% of domestic and 15% of public supply wells fully dewatered (Results, Fig. 3). || Equity: 193 disadvantaged communities (about 2.8 million people) lie in the study area; nearly 40% (1,051 of 2,752) of drinking water wells inside their boundaries are vulnerable, a rate similar to non-disadvantaged areas, while 31 communities in 11 plans have at least half of their area outside monitoring networks and about 15% of wells in disadvantaged communities (n = 508) lie outside the networks (Results, Figs. 4-5). || About 90% of drinking water wells fall inside monitoring networks, but 8 plans cover under 80% of wells, with Eastern San Joaquin covering only 54% (Results, Fig. 4).

outcomes: Storm outcomes: 14 million residents on boil water notices, at least three days longer without potable water in very small systems, and documented gaps in communication, critical-infrastructure power prioritization and emergency alerts.
findings: The paper synthesizes the interconnected impacts on Texas' water and energy resources and infrastructure during Winter Storm Uri (2021), including cascading effects, and evaluates government preparedness, communication, policies and response (abstract). || Of the 14 million residents who were on boil water notices, those served by very small water systems went on average at least three days longer without potable water (abstract). || Available county-level data do not indicate that vulnerable communities went longer periods without power or water, but more resolved data are needed to understand who was most heavily affected at the community or neighborhood level (abstract). || Gaps in government communication, response and policy include difficulty identifying, and securing power to, critical infrastructure and inconsistent use of the state's Emergency Alert System; the authors recommend research on reliable communication, disproportionate impacts on vulnerable communities, health impacts, water infrastructure resilience and climate change effects (abstract).

outcomes: SD-6 LEMA, first decade: pumping goal of -20% exceeded (water use about -25%), depletion rate down about 65%, farm net income not significantly affected (corn cash flow +33%); program renewed to 2027 without further cuts.
findings: In its first decade the Sheridan 6 (SD-6) LEMA, a 255 km2 area of northwest Kansas with water-level declines of up to about 9 m since 1980, exceeded its 20% pumping reduction goal and cut aquifer depletion rates by about 65% without significantly affecting farmers' net income; irrigators committed to a five-year allocation of 140 cm of applied water per hectare, about 20% below the 2002-2012 average of about 36 cm/ha per year (abstract; sect. 2, accepted manuscript). || Under similar climate, water use was about 25% lower in 2013-2022 than in 2002-2012; efficiency improvements gave 72% of the reduction, switching to lower-demand crops (sorghum, wheat) 19% and reduced irrigated area 9% over the first seven years, and about 90% of the reduction came from corn irrigation (sect. 3). || Energy and income: corn producers in the LEMA had 33% higher cash flow despite a corn yield about 1% lower than neighbors; over the first five years cash flow was US$2.24 million above business as usual because energy expenses fell US$2.85 million while gross revenue fell US$0.60 million, and a farm-census analysis shows total expenditures (energy, fertilizer, chemicals) down 45% (sect. 3). || Limits: the roughly 25% pumping cut could extend the aquifer's median usable lifespan by 25-35 years (high uncertainty), but declines continue at a moderated pace, and farmers renewed the LEMA for 2018-2022 and 2023-2027 without further cuts in allocations (sect. 3). || Governance tenets: bottom-up rulemaking with top-down enforcement (99% of nondomestic wells in the groundwater management district metered by 2010, 11 public hearings over four years, fines of US$1,000 per day and a two-year suspension of water rights above a 4.93 ML overuse threshold), a five-year multi-year cap for flexibility, and a management area with homogeneous conditions; the USDA Risk Management Agency devised a limited-irrigation crop insurance agreement because 'good farming practice' rules tied to historical irrigation can discourage conservation (sect. 4).
